speechtext:
On
Monday last the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Huffman) asked two questions with reference to an aircraft firing range on Lake Erie, which I should like now to answer. His first question was:
Has agreement between the Canadian Department of National Defence and the war department of the United States in establishing a firing range for jet and other types of planes using live ammunition on lake Erie been concluded?
The answer is: Yes. Such an agreement was entered into by an exchange of notes between the two countries in October last and runs until December 31, 1952, when it may or may not be renewed by mutual consent.
The second question was:
Why was all the area established north of the international boundary, as indicated by a plan in the London Free Press under date of March 15?
As a matter of fact the area depicted by the London Free Press is not accurate, but the whole area of the firing range is on the Canadian side of the international boundary. It was so arranged in order that complete jurisdiction and control might rest with one country, in this case Canada. The area is well clear of the shore line, and adequate safety precautions will govern its use so that the safety of persons and property outside the area will be in no way endangered.

The house resumed, from Wednesday, March 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Knight:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada, by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock last evening I had explained why we were supporting this motion, and I wish now to review briefly the points which, I suggest, provide convincing reasons why the government should be prepared to accept the motion and take action which will carry out its intent without in any way infringing upon the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial governments in the field of education.
It is not the duty, nor is it the right, of the parliament of Canada to interfere directly or indirectly with any aspect of education itself. Education, however, is everybody's business and everybody's concern. As Canadians, and as members of this house, education must be of great concern to all of us. To the extent that the government and parliament of Canada have it within their power to assure that the provincial governments will have adequate financial resources to give equality of educational

Education
opportunity to children, we in this house should do what we can to make sure that steps will be taken by the government to give the provinces adequate revenues to meet their constitutional obligations.
No problem is causing greater concern to educational and municipal authorities today than that of meeting the heavily increased costs of education. Because of their inability to raise the salaries of teachers, and because they see no immediate prospect of finding the money to do so, unless there is some change in the situation neither the educational nor the municipal authorities will be able to offer that encouragement which would stop the steady and increasingly rapid drain upon the teacher supply in this country.
I pointed out yesterday that the estimate of the bureau of statistics is that if the present drain on teachers continues there will be a shortage of 25,000 teachers by 1955. That would mean disaster to the whole structure of education within Canada. At the same time I pointed out that this estimate is based upon the present percentage of attendance of pupils. The percentage of attendance and the length of time during which the pupils attend are far from satisfactory. As indicated by the figures I gave yesterday, pupils are leaving school far too soon, for many reasons. That flow of pupils from the schools will be increased if because of a shortage of teachers there is more crowding of our classrooms and less opportunity to give the pupils personal attention. If we were able across the whole of Canada to give every child the educational opportunities it should have, and to give equality of education up to the extent of the capacity of every child regardless of the means of its parents or where the child may live, then instead of a shortage of 25,000 we probably would have a shortage of 50,000 teachers by 1955.
I can only repeat that the whole future of this country is dangerously threatened by the possibility that the ten provinces of Canada may not be able to provide the kind of education that has carried us along the road of advancement as far as we have gone. It is not a case of advancing education still farther; the danger is imminent that education will go back rather than ahead, because of a shortage of teachers, and because of the increasing difficulty encountered by municipal and educational authorities in providing the money to meet heavy educational costs.
It is for that reason, because it is of concern to us as well as to the provinces, that I repeat, with all the earnestness I can put into my words, the suggestion that the dominion government arrange to meet the provinces for discussions, now long overdue, in an effort

so to readjust taxation within Canada that the provincial governments may have from their own revenues financial resources which will be adequate to give their children that equality of educational opportunity which I am sure every hon. member in this house wants to see in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In rising to take part in this debate I think I should at the outset make it clear that I am speaking to,a private member's resolution, and not to a government resolution or concerning federal government policy.
It is commonplace to say that the jurisdiction of provincial legislatures over education is, of all provincial rights, the one of which some if not all of the provinces are most jealous. Therefore, as between federal and provincial governments, the initiative in connection with matters pertaining to education is one which I think the federal government has always felt should be taken by the provincial governments. So far as I am aware, the provincial governments have never raised with the federal government at any time the subject matter of this resolution as such; nor have they raised the question of educational costs except as an item of the provincial budgets which naturally were the subject of discussion in the Rowell-Sirois report, in the conference dealing with the dominion proposals of 1945, and indeed in all the fiscal conferences between the federal government and the provinces.
It is for this reason that the federal government as such has never had occasion to consider as a matter of government policy the precise subject matter of the resolution before us. It is quite true, as I have already indicated, that in other contexts this question has arisen. I have no doubt that some of my colleagues have formed opinions upon it, as I have done. The ideas which I express today are, therefore, entirely my own, although doubtless most of my colleagues will agree with some of them.
I should like to compliment all of those who have taken part in this excellent debate, in that they have made clear many points of law and fact which are involved in this resolution. I think it is also correct to say that they have come within striking distance of the nub of the whole matter, although with great respect I do not think that they have actually pin-pointed what that nub is.
From what has been said it is clear that certain points of agreement have emerged. It is hardly necessary for example to repeat all the truisms about the great importance of

education in our national life. Nor is it necessary to argue at great length that teachers' salaries in general are inadequate; for their inadequacy is clearly established by the relative economic unattractiveness of the teaching profession. It is very gratifying to me to hear the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) and the hon. members for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight), Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) state in such positive terms not only that education is wholly a provincial responsibility under the British North America Act, but that it is unthinkable that it should be otherwise. When the hon. member for Red Deer asserted that no child should be deprived of an opportunity to acquire a good education, he was again stating a truism with which no one would disagree. It may be stated that the general agreement in this house upon most of the principles which have been enunciated so far in this debate affords a much more satisfactory basis for examination of the facts than would be the case if we were in disagreement on those principles.
Having stated some of those points of agreement, perhaps I should clear up some of the points upon which I must confess reluctantly I am in disagreement with some hon. members. I disagree, for example, with the leader of the opposition when he states that because the federal government makes grants to the universities of Canada, it admits that it could and should make substantial grants to the provincial governments earmarked for the support of primary education.
In this connection the hon. member made much of the fact that under the British North America Act the provincial legislatures have exclusive jurisdiction over the subject matter of education. That, of course, is quite correct. I suggest that anyone with a reasonable knowledge of Canadian history must realize that it is one thing to make, to universities which are entirely self-governing and non-political, grants which form a minor part of their total income; but it is quite another thing to make, as has been suggested, a contribution which would be a large part of the income of the primary schools of the province, to provincial governments whose provincial departments of education actively control, supervise and make policy for the whole primary school system of the province. There is no comparison between those two facts, and the hon. member draws an analogy which I must regard as a false one.
It was not an accident that at the time of confederation the legislatures of the provinces were given exclusive authority to make laws in relation to education. It was a deliberate provision which certain of the fathers of confederation insisted upon as a
Education
condition to the formation of Canada, in order to protect their religion, their language, and their way of life. The point of this is that primary education is concerned entirely with the instruction of the young during the highly formative period of their life-instruction which, as the Rowell-Sirois report said, is of decisive importance as regards religious training and the preservation of language and of culture. I quote from volume II of the report, page 50:
We have already said that the instruction of the young during their formative years is a matter which the provinces must continue to control- subject, of course, to the safeguard for religious minorities provided in the British North America Act and amendments. A free hand in something so important to the social and cultural life of the people seems to us to be vital to any provincial autonomy worthy of the name, and it is obvious that any attempts to alter the existing arrangements would1 meet with powerful opposition and would provoke profound resentment.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that to anyone who stops to reflect upon this matter the difficulty about large federal educational grants to the provinces earmarked for primary education would be this. If they were large enough to be worth while, the dominion treasury simply could not defend handing out these large sums of money to the provincial governments without assuming some responsibility as to the manner in which they would be spent. For the federal government-for example, the present federal government, or any federal government that might be in power in Canada at some future time-to supervise the manner in which these grants would be spent by a provincial government for primary education would involve, in the opinion of a large number of sincere	Canadians-amongst
whom I number myself as one-an interference with the exclusive authority of the provincial legislatures over education, and something which, under certain governments and under certain circumstances, could prove to be exceedingly harmful. It is for that reason, Mr. Speaker, that, with the leader of the opposition, I think it is preferable that the federal government, rather than make grants to the provinces earmarked for primary education-if the federal government is to provide assistance at all-should provide other financial resources.
On that point the leader of the opposition and I are in complete agreement; and we are supported by the Rowell-Sirois report, which has this to say at page 51-and I quote at some length because this is the definitive recommendation of the report on this very point:
Many representations have been made to us that financial help should be extended by the dominion to the provinces for various purposes, such as scholarships, technical training, grants to be used

Education
for general educational purposes provided1 that the provinces did not reduce their own expenditure on education. These representations appear to have been inspired largely by consternation at the reductions in educational expenditure which certain provinces, under the stress of the depression, have felt compelled to make. It has even been contended that the dominion is bound to see that there is equal educational opportunity, as far as is practicable, for every Canadian child.
We have the deepest sympathy for these views which have been advanced by many of the organizations most closely associated with education in Canada, and we share to the full the regret that, especially in recent years, education has been terribly neglected in many of the poorer parts of the country and that wholly disproportionate sacrifices have been imposed on those who have devoted their lives to this important public service. But the representations appear to us to go too far in denying-
And this, Mr. Speaker, I suggest is the point of this particular part of my argument. -the right of each province to decide the relative importance of expenditure on education and expenditure on other competing services. It is our hope that provision can be made for the fiscal needs of all provinces, including within those needs provision for the education of the young. Our financial proposals-
That is, the financial proposals which the Rowell-Sirois commission outlined in another part of their report.
-aim at placing every province in a position to discharge its responsibilities for education, on a scale that is within the means of the people of Canada, if it chooses to do so. Once this position Is established it seems to us best that education, like every other form of welfare service in a democratic community, should have to fight for its life, and that a generous provision for the education of the children of the nation should depend, not on any arbitrary constitutional provision, but on the persistent conviction of the mass of the people that they must be ready to deny themselves some of the good things of life in order to deal fairly by their children. Hence we do not think that it would be wise or appropriate for the dominion to make grants to the provinces earmarked for the support of general education.
As is well known, Mr. Speaker, owing to the recalcitrance of certain provincial governments, the Sirois recommendations were not put into effect in Canada-that is to say, their financial provisions which were designed to place all the provinces in such a position that, if they wished to do so, they could finance education adequately. Hon. members will also recall that the further recalcitrance of certain provinces prevented the implementation of the proposals made by this federal government in the year 1945 to place the provinces in that position.

Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that the minister at this point retain some semblance of the facts. If he will cast his mind back, he will recall that the provinces met the dominion government in 1946 as well.

opinion, and I do not agree with my hon. friend.
Upon the break-down of these two efforts to put the provinces in such a position that they could adequately deal with what is really their constitutional responsibility, the members of the house are all familiar with the fact that there were negotiated the dominion-provincial tax agreements-which have now been in existence for some four years and which will shortly expire, to be replaced, I hope, by renewal tax agreements even more favourable to the provinces. I shall endeavour to show today that those tax agreements have put the provinces of Canada in such a position that they and their municipalities, if they wish to do so, can increase their support of primary education. But if the municipalities and the provinces having the benefits under these tax agreements, instead of increasing grants to primary education, prefer to increase their expenditures upon roads and bridges, or to reduce debt, or to spend their revenues on the discharge of any other provincial function which they regard as having priority to education, I suggest to the leader of the opposition that they are at perfect freedom, under the tax agreements and under the constitutional law of this country, to exercise that discretion. I am sure that is a freedom which he, having regard to his views on provincial autonomy, would be the first to support and approve.
Therefore, sir, the real question here is whether the federal government and the provinces, in concluding these tax agreements, have attained one of their objectives namely that of placing the provinces in a position, if

they chose to do so, of supporting adequately the cause of primary education. I do not know any shorter or simpler method of establishing that than by pointing out that the provincial authorities, after attending several conferences-the ones arising out of the Rowell-Sirois report; the one, as the leader of the opposition has pointed out, in 1945, extending into 1946, dealing with the proposals of the federal government at that time-after thoroughly canvassing this whole question in those conferences and again in all of the subsequent conferences leading up to the tax agreements themselves, have accepted and executed these agreements. These provincial representatives, who, whatever may be implied to the contrary sometimes. in this house, are very intelligent and competent men, have executed these agreements as purporting to do, and as I think I can show, as in fact doing that very thing; that is, these tax agreements put the provinces in the position of adequately supporting education if they desire to do so.
Some may say that that is a short and simple answer, but not a satisfactory one, that we should have a more objective one. What are the facts and the figures? I do not wish to go too much into detail on the facts and figures, but it so happens, to begin with, that I have some figures applicable to Manitoba, which I have retained since the time that I was treasurer of that province. They indicate that when we went into this tax agreement our revenues from the various sources which were surrendered were in 1946 a little over $8 million in that year. In place of this, we got, under the agreement, a guaranteed minimum of $13,500,000, and received in the year ended March 31, 1948, about $14,500,000. This enabled us to increase our expenditures for education from $2,800,000 in 1946 to $5,600,000 in 1948. That was one of the first things we did with this increase that we got.
I am not suggesting for a minute that even that provision was adequate; but, Mr. Speaker, under the proposed renewal of this agreement the guaranteed payments are $18,800,000 instead of a little over $8 million, and the adjusted payment for 1952-53 is $20,890,000, nearly $21 million. During this interval in Manitoba-which now, as always, has an economical and careful administration; its budget is one of the smallest among the provincial governments, certainly in western Canada- in Manitoba the total budget went up from $19,250,000 in 1946 to over $33,500,000 in 1949, and I saw the other day that its present budget is $49 million. Will anybody argue that between these two limits of $19 million in
Education
1946 and $49 million in 1952 there is not some elbow room if it were needed for some increase in the provincial contributions to primary education?
I have used the figures in the case of Manitoba because they were the only figures that I had to show the revenue that was being obtained from these tax sources before the agreement went into effect. In that connection I might say this. Outside of the central provinces and British Columbia the productivity of these tax fields in Manitoba was higher than it was in either of the other two prairie provinces at that time, so that our relative benefit between what we had got before and after the signing of the tax agreement was smaller than in some of these other provinces.
I think perhaps the best way to indicate the value of the tax agreements is to set out the position of all the provinces during this five-year period, which is covered by this agreement. First may I, without invidiously mentioning any single one of the provinces, examine what their expenditures were for education during that period, and what their expenditures were for highways and bridges. This is a fair comparison to make of two important provincial expenditures.
In 1939-that is, before the tax agreement was entered into-the total expenditures upon education in all the provinces was $38 million. The total expenditures on highways and bridges amounted to $87-6 million. In 1949 the amount spent on education totalled $154,100,000; on highways and bridges, $251,700,000. Now, let us look at the total budget. The total provincial expenditures in 1939 amounted to $356 million. In 1949, they amounted to $858 million. Does anyone suggest that there is not some elbow room in there if the provincial ministers charged with the constitutional responsibility for dealing with education desired to use it? In the face of these large over-all increases in provincial expenditures, does anyone suggest that some more moneys could not have been paid on education?
But apart from these provincial expenditures, let us look for a moment at the surplus position of the provinces. During the five-year period there was not a single province in Canada that did not have a surplus, and a substantial one. The accumulated current account surplus of all Canadian provinces over that five-year period was not less than $670 million, that is a surplus over and above these expenditures that I have been talking about.
Now, these are the provincial governments which the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. 55704-40$

Education
Knight) suggests that as a matter of dire necessity we should help; that we should interfere with provincial autonomy in order to pay some more money over so that they could discharge their provincial responsibilities.

On a point or order; I at no time suggested that we should interfere with provincial autonomy. I maintained throughout that we did not have to interfere with provincial autonomy to bring about the thing that I request.
No one in the house has suggested it.
Order.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: From his standpoint I think my hon. friend is quite right in what he has said. I think the leader of the opposition is also quite right in his interjection, but I suggest from my standpoint, and I have had some little experience in provincial administration, I should like to know how the federal treasury could pay over large amounts of money to the support of primary education without in practice interfering with provincial autonomy.
I should like to ask the minister a question. Have I his permission?
With the minister's permission.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Certainly.
My question is this: The minister made a great point of the difference between direct grants-
Ask the question.
-to universities as apart from grants to the provinces.
Ask the question.

My question is this, my friend: Is it the minister's considered opinion that the $35 million which has been paid already by the dominion government for the purposes of education, a great part of which has gone to the provinces in the form of indirect vocational and technical aid grants and so on, has interfered in any way with the jurisdiction of the provinces over education within the provinces?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope you will allow me extra time in which to answer these questions. I had thought that I had made that point clear. I tried to make it precise by drawing a clear distinction between payments to the universities of Canada, which are non-political and entirely

self-governing, on the one hand, and payments by the federal government to the provincial governments which are earmarked as grants in aid in respect of a matter that comes under the active control of the provincial departments of education on the other hand. If that distinction does not elucidate the point to my hon. friend's satisfaction, then I am afraid I cannot do any more for him.

What is the answer of the minister? Is it his considered opinion that those grants to the provinces, indirect grants to the provinces for the purposes of education-he has not answered my question-is it his considered opinion that those grants have in no way infringed on minority rights in connection with education?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am quite prepared to answer that question with one word-no. I said in the beginning, I repeated it and I will repeat it now if my hon. friend insists, that there is no comparison between the payments he has just been referring to and large contributions by the federal treasury to the provincial treasurers for the support of primary education. If he will not accept my reasons I ask my hon. friend to agree with the reasons given by the Rowell-Sirois commission.

May I ask a question just to clarify the matter? I understand from the minister that he is suggesting that the expenditures in the different provinces right across Canada have been higher for highways than for education?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
I assure the minister he is not correct, because the expenditures in Ontario-
You made your speech.
I am giving the facts. The expenditures last year in Ontario on highways were $52,267,000 and on education, $67,888,000.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

If it does not illuminate it then the minister is wasting a lot of time.

speechtext: It only goes to show that since my hon. friend's departure from Ontario their policies with regard to expenditures on education have been improved.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The same thing happened in Manitoba.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: All the figures I have used apply to years of my hon. friend's regime.
The minister does not know what he is talking about.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That too is a matter of opinion. I am not able to agree with my hon. friend's opinions always, unfortunately.
Very few can.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But I want to compliment the leader of the opposition upon the excellent speech he made and with the main point of which I agree entirely, that is that if we are going to preserve provincial autonomy it is better to put the provinces in a financial position to support properly their schools and to let them exercise that autonomy by choosing themselves between different outlets for expenditures. But I do not agree with my hon. friend in the precise manner that he advocates for putting the provinces in that position. He says to do away with these tax agreements which have proved in fact to be so beneficial to all the provinces.
Not to Ontario.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He says, "let the dominion government cease invading the provincial fields of taxation."
Correct.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I see my hon. friend has gained at least one adherent for this wrong conception of his. My hon. friend, I should think for a matter of seven or eight years, has been harping upon this business of the federal government invading provincial fields of taxation. I do not expect to change his
Education
views by drawing his attention to the provisions of the British North America Act because he has had them drawn to his attention many times before and has remained completely impervious to them. But I would point out to you, sir, that section 91 says this: -it is hereby declared that . . . the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated, that is to say,-
3. The raising of money by any mode or system of taxation.
I apologize to the house for putting to it a proposition which, but for the views which have been disseminated in this house by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition would be an insult to the intelligence of hon. members. The proposition is this: Since the powers of the parliament of Canada with regard to the imposition of taxation are completely unlimited, in what sense can it be said that parliament invades any other legislature's field of taxation by exercising powers which the constitution gives to parliament?
I will answer that. .
Order.
It is a question.
Sit down.
I understood it was a question.
Sit down.
With the minister's permission.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is all right.
I took it as a question and I am very happy to answer it.
You are not making a speech.

The answer is very simple. At the time the dominion government asked the provinces to enter into agreements during the course of the war whereby the provinces would remain out of certain tax fields, they did so with the unqualified promise that after the termination of the war those tax fields would be returned to them undiminished. The government is in default on its solemn word, and has been ever since.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, that is a very interesting piece of special pleading; but it is, it so happens, rather a complete refutation of what my hon. friend has just said, that the parties to this wartime tax suspension agreement, with the exception of two provinces-
Which embrace over 60 per cent of the population.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
-entered into tax agreements under which they have agreed, not to give

Education
up their power of taxation but merely not to exercise those powers during the currency of those agreements, in return for payments from the dominion treasury which are much larger than the signing provinces were ever able to obtain from those taxes themselves at any time in their previous financial history.
And, so far as the other two provinces of Ontario and Quebec are concerned, at the very same time my hon. friend made the statement he just made a moment ago, these provinces are themselves occupying these fields of provincial taxation of which he speaks, not having signed tax agreements. So that my hon. friend's elucidation of his position today has not added anything to the positions that he has previously taken on it. And these positions have never had any foundation in constitutional law.
On a point of order, I did not realize that we were discussing taxation agreements. I thought we were discussing education.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, I should have thought the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), having regard to the fact that the provinces have the responsibility for the financing of education, would regard perhaps as being related to that question the fact that the tax agreements help to put the provinces in the funds with which to discharge that responsibility.
The reference to it was all right, but let us not have a debate on it.
It was a lengthy reference.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: So far as the provinces of Ontario and Quebec are concerned, I would say there is a most interesting article in the Toronto Saturday Night of March 1 which tends to show that these existing tax agreements, thie ones that are expiring, were so favourable to the provinces that even the provinces of Ontario and Quebec have lost substantially by not signing them.
That is not so.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, my hon, friend knows it all, of course. I was referring to the article in the Toronto Saturday Night; and if my hon. friend will forgive my saying so, I would rather take their views than his in the matter.
You need to be educated'.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
At the time when a renewal of the tax agreements is being considered, it is absolutely open to all the provinces, the whole ten of them, to decide whether they will come into the agreements or stay out of them. And, if they stay out, then, in the case of

the two central provinces, they will continue to do what they have been doing for the last five years, and that is to occupy perfectly freely and in the same way as they always did the fields of provincial taxation, to the extent that they wish to do so. And they can continue that position.
Now, in view of the expenditures by provincial governments upon subject matters other than education, in view of the surplus position over the five-year period of some $670 million by way of surplus on current account-and that is over two-thirds of a billion-it seems to be reasonable to suggest that, if they wished1 to do so, they could increase expenditures upon primary education. They could increase those expenditures out of their present resources, instead of reducing debts, instead of having surpluses, instead of having built so many roads, and1 so on. And if we are going to pay the respect to provincial rights and to provincial autonomy that we should pay, then it seems to me that once the provinces have been placed in that favourable financial position, one which has improved out of all recognition over what it was prior to these tax agreements, and improved not only because of the tax agreements but also as a result of other federal policies, which have increased greatly the productivity of the provincial taxes themselves-
And yours has, too.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is quite right, yes. Also in the interval our necessity for expenditures has not only increased but has been multiplied, and the burden under which the federal budget is now labouring is an enormous one, as I am sure my hon. friend will agree.
A lot of people will agree with that.
The taxpayers of Canada realize it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
And, for that reason, the point of this whole matter seems to be this, that so long as the provincial governments have exclusive jurisdiction over the subject of education, which they will continue to have, then they should have the right, to use the language of the Sirois report, to decide the relative importance of expenditures on education and expenditures upon other competing provincial services.
They have that because, again to use the language of the Sirois report, a generous provision for the education of the children of the nation depends, in the last analysis, not upon any arbitrary constitutional provision, but upon the persistent conviction of the mass

of the people that they must be ready to deny themselves some of the good things of life in order to deal fairly with their children.
It is in precisely the realm of political activity of the municipalities and the provinces, which are continually being held up to us as being closer to the people, that these decisions are made, and that the impact of the people's views can be brought most forcibly upon those who have decisions to make.
Once it is the fact-and it is the fact- that the provincial treasuries are no longer in the position in which they were prior to these tax agreements, it can no longer be argued that they are unable to make these provisions, if they wish to do so. And if therefore the people of the provinces, speaking democratically through their votes, really want a lot of money spent on education, it is a simple matter for them to elect provincial governments pledged to spend it instead of attempting to throw yet another burden upon the sorely pressed federal government, and at the same time in my view-and I think in this the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) will agree with me-attempting to make a really vital attack upon provincial autonomy.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure provincial governments across Canada will appreciate the lecture the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) has just given them. It makes one wonder why the minister has changed his opinion so greatly since the days when he himself was a member of a provincial government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Provincial treasurer, at that.

And it makes one
wonder-

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: On a question of privilege I would simply affirm-and I hope my hon. friend will accept my statement-that my views have not changed at all; they are precisely the same now as they were then. What has changed is the financial position of the provinces.

It makes one wonder how it comes about that the minister knows the needs of the province so much better than the premier of that province. Those are questions which naturally come to mind of one who does not know much about the inner working of Liberal politics.
This subject of federal aid to education to my knowledge has been before the house almost annually for the last ten years. I first spoke here in support of federal aid to education back in 1942, and I do not think there has been a year since when there has not been a debate on that subject in this house in one form or another. The arguments
Education
for federal aid to education have been presented to the house year after year. Every hon. member who has given any thought to this subject knows those arguments. Every hon. member who has been in contact with his municipal council and his school boards knows those arguments and knows how necessary is federal aid to education. Every member of this house who has considered the matter knows that just as we passed from the stage when the municipal taxpayer was called upon to bear the entire cost of education, so now we have reached a point where the cost of education should no longer be left to the municipal taxpayer and the provincial government. Every hon. member knows that without federal aid the governments of some of the provinces just cannot provide educational opportunities equal to those provided by other provinces. In spite of all the minister may say about expenditures on roads and bridges instead of education, in spite of all he may say about what the provincial governments could do for education if they wanted, he knows that no matter how sincere some provincial governments may be in attempting to provide equal educational opportunities for their children they just cannot do it.
We who support federal aid to education maintain, and we think quite rightly, that it is the heritage of every Canadian child to be given the best educational opportunities that are available, not in Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick or Newfoundland or Quebec or any other province, but the best educational opportunities that can be provided by Canada as a nation. That is the basis on which we make our claim for federal support for education. As a matter of fact I doubt whether many measures that have come before this house in recent years have had more public support across Canada than this matter of federal aid to education. The parents of this country are interested in it. They are much more interested in getting the best possible education for their boys boys and girls than in any quarrel the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) may have with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), or in any quarrels between political parties in this country in regard to federal and provincial jurisdiction or the taxing rights of the provincial and federal governments. What the parents of this country want is that regardless of where those children may live, they shall be given the opportunity to get the best in education this country can offer. They are quite willing to let the politicians fight their battles over questions of provincial and federal rights. They expect us as intelligent representatives of the people to

Education
get together with the provincial authorities and find some formula which will give the children that educational opportunity.
I said few measures had received more popular support than this. Home and school associations all across this country, who know educational problems and are interested in education, have supported this measure. School trustee associations, municipal councils, trade union congresses, farmer organizations, chambers of commerce and, I am told, at least five provincial governments support federal aid for education. I know some provinces have requested it. The premier of Manitoba, the minister's own province, is on record at the federal-provincial conference of last fall as asking for federal aid for education. This measure has been receiving increasing support across the country because the need has been growing and becoming more evident every year. Now we are actually facing a crisis. It may be quite true, as the minister says, that the provincial governments are delinquent in their duty towards education, that they are not conscious of the need-

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend knows I did not say the provincial governments were delinquent in their duty, so he should not attribute the statement to me.

O.K.; the provincial
premiers can read what the minister said. They can read his lecture on their willingness to spend more money on roads and bridges than on education. They can see where he pointed out that if they wanted to spend more money on education they could do so. His words are there to be read. But whether or not the minister is right, the fact is that a crisis is developing. If the present trend continues until 1955, as was pointed out yesterday, by that time we shall have a shortage of 25,000 teachers. That means that in 1955 half a million boys and girls in Canada will be without teachers in their schools. That is a very serious matter. Whether the provincial governments or the federal government may be responsible for education, the thing we have to consider here is whether we as a nation can afford to let half a million of our children go without teachers. The parents of those children are not concerned with our quarrel over constitutional questions. It is the job of the politicians to iron out those difficulties. That is where the federal government should show some initiative in getting together with the provinces. We have done that in other fields. It would not be the first time the federal government has had to 
go into a huddle with the provinces to arrive at some agreement by which the federal government would come to their aid.
The minister has drawn a whole school of red herring across the trail in his effort to indicate to the Liberal members of this house how the government wants them to vote on this issue. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this is a matter far too important to Canada as a nation to be one in which members of any party should take cabinet dictation. This is a matter upon which every member in the house should be entirely free to vote as he feels will be in the best interest of the boys and girls of today, who will be the citizens of tomorrow.
We are not asking for a vote of confidence in the government. We are not suggesting that the federal government should step in and take over control of education. Other civilized countries in the world today, with the federal system of government, find it possible for the central government to give the amount of money that the Minister of Justice was talking about without infringing upon state or provincial rights. They have been doing it for years. This argument that the federal government cannot put any sizeable sum into the hands of the province for educational purposes without interfering with what religion is taught in the schools is just so much boloney. It is done in other countries, and it can be done in this country if the iLiberal government wants to do it. It can be done without any interference with religion, language or anything else that is taught in the schools of the various provinces.
All we are asking for in this resolution is that, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada, by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces. We are asking the government to take that matter into consideration. I presume that means getting together with the provinces, and attempting to find out if there is not some way whereby the federal government can co-operate with the provinces in a manner that will be acceptable to the provinces. Then, the federal government could make it possible for boys and girls living in one province during the early years of their life to be educated as Canadian citizens, and not as citizens of any one province. It would make it possible for them to move from one province to another, equipped educationally to the best possible extent that Canada can afford, and not merely to the extent that a particular province or municipality can afford.

It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the first step towards

equalizing opportunity of education should come from the provinces themselves. School boards in districts with low assessment find a great deal of difficulty in providing adequate funds for teachers' salaries, and for capital expenditures. In the case of the province of Ontario, with which I am familiar, that problem has been attacked in a very realistic way. Because I am familiar with the way that problem has been tackled, I propose to mention it here.
In Ontario, the government not only gives a fixed sum for each pupil in average attendance during the preceding year, but also gives supplementary grants on a sliding scale whereby districts with the smallest population and the lowest assessment receive the largest grants. In this way Ontario strives to equalize the opportunity for education within the province. Now, I believe that the federal government should make funds available on a sliding scale to help equalize the opportunity for education between the provinces, in the same way as Ontario has made funds available to equalize opportunities within the province. It would not be my intention that the federal government should take any part in the policy or administration of education. This field belongs to the provinces alone.
This government should beware also of attaching any strings to grants which it might make, lest those grants become a factor in policy making. However, at the present time, the federal government makes grants to education without encroaching upon the sovereignty of the provinces. I believe it could do a great deal more.
The greatest variations in opportunity for education come from two sources. First, there is inequality in the physical facilities for education. Second, there is inequality in the standards of teaching. The first of these we shall always have with us, because it is impossible to provide in small rural communities the great variety of facilities available in large centres. This difference can be best modified by the governments closest to the needs of the people.
However, the unequal standards of teaching we do not need to accept. I believe it is here that federal funds will be of the greatest assistance. They would not interfere with the policy or administration of education within a province, but would make available to the poorer provinces additional funds so that they could bring their teachers' salaries up to the level of those of the wealthier provinces.
Surely, it is the policy of all provincial governments to hire the most qualified teachers that they can afford. Unfortunately,
Education
there is often not sufficient money available to hire highly qualified teachers, and funds for the purpose of equalizing the standards of teachers' salaries would do more for the equalization of opportunity in education than anything else. A poor teacher in a well equipped school cannot give a sound education; but a good teacher in a poorly equipped school can achieve wonders.
Let us, therefore, make funds available so that each province can give its teachers in all districts a salary sufficient to recompense them for undergoing the long training necessary to become good teachers; a salary sufficient to entice into that vitally important field the many able and interested people who at present must shun the teaching profession simply because of the inadequate salary which that profession provides. In this way the federal government would be in no way interfering with the rights of the provinces, and it would be a long step towards making the equalization of opportunity for education a reality.
I should like to make a further suggestion which would probably be contingent upon greater funds being made available to the provinces for more highly trained teachers. I believe that school boards should give serious consideration to the matter of a more intensive study of French and English in all grades. Our country is bilingual by law, but in most regions it is not bilingual in practice. The two languages are often a purely mechanical barrier between the two great races working out a better understanding with each other. If all children from grade 1 up were taught both languages, this mechanical barrier would disappear; and with the greater understanding of each other, closer unity would, I believe, result.
Another matter within the federal field of education is the need for the establishment of a tri-services college within the province of Quebec, without in any way encroaching upon provincial rights. I attended the Royal Military College between the years 1927 and 1931. When I was there I felt that it was a great pity that more French-speaking Canadians did not attend that college. The obvious reason they did not attend it was the language difficulty. The few who did attend were up against a very real handicap indeed.
Today, of the 500 cadets in the two service colleges, only 38 are French-speaking Canadians. It is obviously preferable that all potential officers should be trained together at the same college. But if French-speaking Canadians do not come forward in sufficiently large numbers because of language

Education
difficulties, I believe that the sensible thing to do is to establish a separate services college in the province of Quebec.
During the war I served in two brigades with two French-Canadian regiments. Their valour and efficiency were equal to any in the Canadian army. I believe that we must do everything we can to make it as easy as possible for large numbers of French-speaking officers to be trained in preparation for another possible conflict. The way to do this is, I believe, through the establishment of a tri-services college in the province of Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I am in the unenviable position that I have just been preceded by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), who has stolen about half of the speech that I wished to make today. I wish, however, to point out to some of the hon. members the difference between aid to universities and aid for technical training and general education. It must be admitted by all here that we need scientific education in the development of Canada. We are fast becoming an industrial nation. In order to support this industry and to develop as have other countries with more experience, we must train the people. This is a national matter. The help that we can, by the dominion, give the universities in technical training to workmen is justified. When we come to the provinces, however, we have provinces that want to give various types of education. We have some provinces that want to educate their children longer than do others. If we step into the field of general education, the government would have to set certain standards that must be lived up to before they could make contributions.
I note that the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) rightly suggested that the schools should teach more French and English. I think that is an excellent idea. But is he not here in the federal house laying down a law for the various provinces to follow? And that is just the sort of thing that would happen if we got into the field of education.
A few years ago I certainly could have supported aid for general education to the west and to the maritimes because of the sparseness of their population; they had long distances to go and small taxes, and that aid would have been justified. But I think the picture is changing, and doing so rapidly. With the discovery of oil and mineral resources, and the coming industrialization of the west and the maritimes these people will have the money; and they have the money, as has been indicated by the Minister of Justice. All have surpluses and they can pay for education if they so choose. I agree

with the Minister of Justice that for us to hand over large sums of money to the provinces for manipulation by the provinces themselves would be a mistake. They have the money. Let them spend it where they wish. If we handed them over large sums of money, they might withdraw all money from education and let us pay for it. That would not make sense.
I am, of course, particularly familiar with the province of Ontario, which has a $30 million surplus this year. Why do they not use that $30 million surplus to better education in the province? As a matter of fact, education in the province of Ontario today is responsible for the most profligate wastage that has ever occurred in that province. I could give some examples where the amount spent on schools, at the insistence of the board of education in Toronto, was twice that which the local boards wanted to spend but which they had to spend or they could not get the grant. I am thinking of gymnasiums, auditoriums, swimming pools-yes, even a sound-proof rifle range. That is not the sort of thing that the federal government wants to pay money for. They want to pay money for education.
Do not misunderstand me. I believe in auditoriums, gymnasiums, swimming pools- yes, even a rifle range-in the crowded cities in order that we may keep the children off the streets, keep them occupied and give them something. But how ridiculous it is to provide, for the children of agricultural people, auditoriums, swimming pools and all those things when they have available the great out-of-doors; when they leave school at four o'clock they can go back and get the best education in the world on their own farms. I would hate to see the money go to such a place as the province of Ontario, having regard to the way they have forced these small municipalities practically into bankruptcy by insisting that they take on this terrific burden of education.
You should go out to Saskatchewan.

The type and the amount of education that should take place in the province is for government at its lowest level to decide; it is not something to be decided by a department of education in the capital of some province, and which insists that the local authorities do this, that and the other thing. They should have a certain standard of health, and if they provide this standard of health, let them proceed from there, not tell them that they are going to build gymnasiums, swimming pools and rifle ranges, as has been done. Let them build their own.
That is what Thomson says.
That is what he said.
See what he got.

If the provinces would forget the concentration on the frills and would go in for more technical education for which there is available to them the help of the federal government, we would be making a contribution to Canada as a whole. That is what this house is interested in: Canada as a whole. We should not invade provincial rights and we certainly should not provide money to be used on the type of frills that are being provided in Ontario today.

Mr. Speaker, we do not want to see this motion talked out. Consequently we are omitting to say a lot of things on the subject that we might say. In listening to the hon. member who has just spoken, I noted that he raised the old bogey of provincial rights. I do not see that the question of provincial rights has much effect having regard to what the resolution of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) is looking for. All that resolution asks for, in so far as the federal government can do it by way of grants in aid, is the endeavour to equalize educational opportunities of all children in Canada. The hon. member who has just taken his seat definitely proved the necessity for action of that kind. His whole argument was that Ontario has too much money, that they are throwing it away on unnecessary gadgets, and so forth. That is exactly what this resolution deals with. It recognizes the inability of the provinces all across this country, because of the difference in provincial income, to be able to do the things in the educational field that they would like to do.
If the federal government adopted the resolution that is on the order paper, there is no reason why some of the surplus that Ontario has could not be used in Prince Edward Island, in New Brunswick and in other sections of Canada where salaries are very low in comparison with what they are in Ontario.
The hon. member said he believed in Canada as a whole. That is exactly what the resolution is asking him to do.
You might use the surplus in Quebec.
And the federal surplus, too.

His whole argument was in
support of the resolution, although he thought he was arguing against it. I feel strongly
Education
on this subject because within the past few months in the section of Canada that I come from we had teachers of the rural sections driven to the point that, in order to focus attention on their problem, they were obliged to go on strike. That strike lasted I think about six weeks. Thousands of children were home from school-of course the children did not mind that. The salaries in that area were down around $1,100 a year. The teachers received a lot of criticism. It was said that they should not have gone on strike; it was not a dignified thing to do; and so forth and so on. The question had been debated in this parliament, in the provincial legislature and by the municipalities, for years. But the teachers got no action, and so they were forced to do what they did in order to focus public opinion on the question.
I should like to ask some hon. members who say that, by granting federal aid, you are invading provincial rights, you are going to upset the constitution and so forth, how it is that that objection is not raised when the health grants are discussed. It is exactly the same thing. The field of health is under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments. Nevertheless, millions of dollars a year are given in grants in aid to the provinces, and are used for that purpose, and nobody screams about upsetting the constitution or invading provincial rights. It is necessary. Then again, on this matter of aid, whether it is an aid or a subsidy, it is federal government money being used for the purpose of advancing the best interests of the country.
You are subsidizing practically everything in this country. The whole agricultural industry is receiving grants in aid from the federal government, and nobody hollers about provincial rights. Practically every industry in this country is receiving grants in aid from the federal government in one way or another. The railroads get subventions for the movement of steel, coal, grain and so on. They are grants in aid, and nobody talks about the constitutional position. Canadian National Railways receive write-offs ,of theoretical deficits amounting to millions of dollars a year. They are grants in aid to the railroads, and they are applicable to every province in the country, but nobody says anything about provincial rights. But in the field of education, where teachers are moulding the future citizens of this country, they are asked to work for salaries lower than street cleaners receive in some instances. The moment you raise the question of bringing up the individual teacher's salary to the point where he can live everybody screams about invading provincial rights.

Education
There may be something to a theory that I have had for a long time. It is a good thing for those in power to keep as many people in the country in that grade 6 or grade 8 scale as long as they can be kept there. They are hewers of wood and drawers of water. It is not hard to get them into the army to pack a rifle and that kind of thing. It may be dangerous to educate them too highly. Take the last war, and the number of young men who went into the services who were illiterate. The federal government had to set up schools in this country in order to give a large percentage of young men who went into the services the necessary education to be able to sit down and read a map and understand it. There the federal government went into the field of education, but nobody screamed about provincial rights. They took from the provinces hundreds of young men who were illiterate, and in order to place them in a position where they could understand their basic training and read the manuals they had to set up schools.
The provinces have had jurisdiction in that field since confederation, and it has not worked-not to the satisfaction of the people of Canada, and particularly of the teachers. Thousands of young men who came out of the services in the last war, from province to province, found themselves in the position where they could not take advantage of the government's program of rehabilitation. They did not have university entrance, so they were out so far as university training was concerned. Thousands of them, who did not have grade 8 education, could not even take the vocational training end of the program. They were dealt out completely. We demanded in the house-it was demanded in the legislatures-that part of the rehabilitation program should have been to take a boy who was in the sixth or the seventh grade and give him at least sufficient schooling to enable him to take the full program of vocational training. It was not done.
The provinces have not done the job that they should have done. They have not done it because of the unequal distribution of the wealth of the country. Ontario can do it, yes. Eighty per cent of the succession duties paid in this country over the years, until 1949 anyway, were paid in the province of Ontario. Do not think that the big estates were built up of capital all earned in this province. It was earned all over this country, but the estates were built here. The same thing applies to at least one section of Quebec that I know of, namely, Mount Royal.
A lot of the taxes paid in the central provinces comes from money from other parts
[Mr. GiUis.l
of the country. The taxes are paid on it here. I do not think the federal government will do anything about federal aid at this session, but I think it should at least do this. The dominion-provincial agreements are coming up for discussion. I do not think that provinces like Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia are getting the deal they should get, having regard to the provincial income. I do not know about Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia, but I do check the figures for the maritimes, and I do not think they are getting the deal they should. For example, in the 1947 agreements the province of Nova Scotia received from the federal government about $16,300,000. I understand that that includes the statutory subsidies of about $2 million a year. Under the new agreement, which I think has been entered into, or is about to be entered into, they will step that amount up by about $2 million to $18 million. I cannot see Nova Scotia getting the deal there that she should get, because I hold in my hand a press release. It is dated February 16, 1951, and it sets out that in that year the provincial government paid back to the federal government in the fields of taxation which they had relinquished some $24,338,000. I have the details here if the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) wants me to read them, but I never like cluttering up the record with too many statistics. The figures are official as they come from Ottawa. Under the agreement the dominion government paid back to the province $16,800,000. That indicates that there is $8 million to play around with and that would help the Nova Scotia government considerably.
I am not making any demands, because I know there is much more money coming into the province from the federal government than is paid under these agreements. I have always taken the position that the provincial governments which have not made similar arrangements with the federal governments are evading their national responsibility. Family allowances, old age pensions, assistance to those 65 to 69 years of age, subsidies to mining, agriculture and other industries such as steel and what have you, all those come back to the provinces. Somebody pays taxes on those things to the provincial governments of Ontario and Quebec. I repeat that they are not accepting their national responsibility when they refuse to come under these agreements.
While I might make an argument for the payment of that $8 million, I am not going to do it. I mention it merely to show the unreasonable position taken by the central provinces in relation to the equalization of

educational opportunity, social security and so forth across this country. They are not pulling their share of the load.
I am suggesting that if the agreement with Nova Scotia has not been finalized consideration should be given to an upward revision to enable that province to do something about the teachers' salary problem. I spoke about this briefly in the throne speech debate.
I figure that Nova Scotia has reached the end of its rope. To attempt to throw the load on the municipalities is most unreasonable because the municipalities in that part of the country are imposing taxes on property as high as 12 per cent. They just cannot go any further. In the town in which I live 60 per cent of every dollar taken in in taxes is spent on the schools. That town cannot continue to carry that load without cutting down on other services. It just cannot go any further. The salaries paid in the municipalities are as high as the municipalities can pay.
Unless the provincial government can find new sources of revenue, and they are trying -they are talking about a tax on gypsum and so forth-they will not be able to do any more than they are at the present time. Teachers right across the country should receive the same salary. There should be no differential as between provinces because they are all Canadians and doing the same job. In order that that can be done arrangements must be made with the federal government. If Ontario does not want to enter into such arrangements-according to some speakers, Quebec is quite willing to talk over the matter in an effort to come to some understanding- that is fine, but I believe the provinces of this country should receive some consideration in their need.
It amuses me sometimes to hear hon. members say that if we accept money from the federal government that government will soon be writing a uniform curriculum for the schools all across the country. It might be a good thing if they did. About two months ago I listened to a national forum over the air composed of eminent scholars in different localities all the way from Vancouver to Halifax. We heard from people in Halifax, Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba and from a number of other provincial stations. They were discussing the question of the school curriculum in the different provinces.
According to the discussion, the history as taught in Manitoba and in Quebec is absolutely different. It was teachers who were making these statements. For example, they said that the history with regard to the Riel rebellion had a completely different version in Quebec from what was taught in
Education
Manitoba. We talk about national unity, but if we cannot have the same facts of history taught to our children how are we going to have national unity? The whole matter is involved in the field of education.
After attempting to handle this problem since confederation the provinces have demonstrated that all they can do is to set up differentials in salary across the country, to such an extent that the teachers are just walking away from their profession. Young boys and girls who might take up this profession are advised not to do so because there is no future in it.
We are very anxious to have this matter voted on tonight, favourably I hope. There are a lot of things one could say on this subject, but I do not want to be accused of talking it out. I hope other hon. members will make their speeches short and to the point so that we can have a favourable vote and tell the federal government that we want federal aid to education. We can do it without disrupting the constitution or wanting to write the school curriculum for the different provinces.
This federal aid would be just the same as other forms of aid now given to the provinces. It would be administered provincially, but it would be marked specifically for educational purposes. I hope we can have a favourable vote tonight. If Ontario does not want to come in, as was indicated by the last speaker-
He did not speak for Ontario, he spoke for Mr. Thomson.
I am glad to hear he did not.
Just for the minority.

In my opinion the dominion government should be ready to render this assistance.
