Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of taking part in the debate this afternoon, but I feel that the scope of the matter under discussion and the effects which would follow the adoption of such a motion justify my attitude.
The confederation act of 1867 has established the rights and privileges of the different governments and has placed all matters pertaining to education under the unqualified jurisdiction of the provinces. The fathers of confederation, having carefully examined the problem of education, acted very wisely, I think, in denying the federal government jurisdiction over this field of activity. Consequently, the constitution gives the provinces full sovereignty in the field

Education
of education. As long as my province will accept its responsibilities-which I hope she will never shun-I shall object to any interference by the central government in matters over which it has no jurisdiction, especially with regard to education.
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) said a few minutes ago that the provinces should make the first step. However, as the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier) stated yesterday, the province of Quebec has a surplus of funds for educational purposes, and so the chances are that Quebec will never request any grant from the federal government.
For those reasons and for others upon which it is not necessary to elaborate at great length, I am opposed to the present resolution. It has given the hon. members an opportunity to express their views. I am convinced that the Liberal party will reject unanimously such a resolution.
I shall therefore vote against the motion presented by the C.C.F. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) on the grounds that it is too general, that it lacks preciseness and that, in my estimation, it constitutes an unfortunate attempt to encroach upon the field of education, which is and must remain under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces.
(Text):

Mr. Speaker, the subject of education is one of very great importance to everyone in Canada. While we are deliberating here from day to day more than 2,500,000 young Canadians are in attendance at schools and colleges throughout this dominion. Parents, trustees, teachers and provincial governments are devoting close attention to the problem of education.
Despite the allocation of the responsibility for education to the provinces by section 93 of the British North America Act, the dominion government in my opinion has or should have a very great interest in education. One of the great problems of any state is that of national unity. For no country has it been a greater problem than for Canada. The two major racial groups, English and French, joined together in a federation, have the marked characteristics of race, language and religion that at times tend to keep them apart.
The geographical barriers to unity in Canada need no special comment. Superimposed upon these factors that make for disunity has been the steady growth of immigration into this country, based upon policies adopted by the federal government. During the forty-five years from 1896 to
IMr. Gauthier (Lake St. John).]
1941 there were 5 million people from all parts of Europe who entered Canada as immigrants. Less than half of them stayed, owing to the greater attraction south of the border; but a pattern was set, and subsequent immigration has not altered the picture.
We are a diverse people. Nowhere is the diversity of our population more apparent than in western Canada. On some occasions the Winnipeg Free Press has printed New Year's greetings in 67 different languages. The British and Foreign Bible Society has sold the scriptures in the city of Winnipeg in 50 languages. At the present time about 85 per cent of the people are Canadian-born; but we are still too young a country for the influence of racial origin to be ignored.
On the matter of racial origin, the dominion bureau of statistics, according to the census of 1941, indicates that the Irish comprise
11	per cent of our population, the Scots
12	per cent, the English about 25 per cent and the French 30 per cent. The remaining 22 per cent comprise very large groups and numbers of people. In round figures, just to show the extent of the racial origins of groups in Canada, the 1941 census shows that there are 470,000 people of German origin, 310,000 of Ukrainian, 215,000 Nether-landers, 170,000 Jews, 168,000 Poles, 113,000 Italians, 100,000 Norwegians, 85,000 Swedes,
38.000	Danes, 21,000 Icelanders, 84,000 Russians, 43,000 Czechoslovakians, 41,000 Finns, 38,000 Austrians, 30,000 Belgians,
25.000	Roumanians, 22,000 Yugoslavs and
11.000	Greeks, in addition to other smaller national groups from Europe.
Then, we have 75,000 Asiatics, 22,000 Negroes and 125,000 Indians and Eskimos. In 1867, when the British North America Act established the Dominion of Canada the racial groups were divided into 2,110,000 from the British isles, 1,080,000 French,
200.000	Germans, 30,000 Dutch and a negligible number from four other races. So when the fathers of confederation assigned to the provinces the sole responsibility for education the difficulties that were to arise from immigration forty or fifty years later were not envisaged.
To cope with all the inherent forces of disunity in Canada, to weld together into one nation all these diverse groups, the chief influence throughout the last fifty years has been the Canadian provincial school system, and in particular the elementary schools. The process of adaptation, assimilation and integration has of necessity been carried out largely with the descendants of immigrants in the second and third generations, for, on the whole, the task of instructing our immigrant population in Canadian ways has

received no special attention. We have simply assumed that they would wish to learn our languages and adopt our customs. No special effort has been made to inculcate in them a pride in being Canadian. No special effort has been made to emphasize our traditions or to lay stress on Canadian citizenship.
As a result the development of Canadian unity has been retarded. The time has surely come for increasing the emphasis on Canada, its history, its traditions, its heritage and its culture. The making of a Canadian nation is a long, slow process, and it is of national or federal concern. At its base is education, elementary, secondary and university.
The very diversity of our racial origins in this country is a strong argument in favour of just such a survey as has recently been completed by the Massey commission.
You cannot by wishing or direction create a Canadian culture; but you can certainly provide by forethought for its development. Provide the means; make suitable the environment and the arts, letters and sciences will develop.
The preamble to the terms of reference of the Massey commission reads in part as follows:
That it is desirable that the Canadian people should know as much as possible about their country, its history and traditions: and about their national life and common achievements.
The report goes on to state this clearly implies-
-that there are important things in the life of a nation which cannot be weighed or measured. These intangible elements are not only essential in themselves; they may serve to inspire a nation's devotion and to prompt a nation's action.
Then follows this important passage:
When Winston Churchill in 1940 called the British people to their supreme effort he invoked the traditions of his country and based his appeal on the common background from which had grown the character and way of life of his fellow countrymen. In the spiritual heritage of Great Britain was found the quickening force to meet the menacing facts of that perilous hour. Nothing could have been more "practical" than that appeal to thought and emotion.
If a similar appeal to thought and emotion could be made in Canada by an emphasis on our history and traditions it would serve us well in our slow march toward unity within the state; and that emphasis is of federal importance and concern. The most readily available agency for imparting knowledge of our history and traditions is the school system. The federal authority has a great interest in the education of the Canadian people.
Education
On a lower plane the federal authority is concerned with the standard of education of our people. There is a close relation between the lack of education and the committing of serious crimes. Our federal prisons are evidence of that fact, for the present inmates are largely those who have had very little formal education in our schools. During the last war the federal authorities discovered an unusually large number of illiterates or semiilliterates, who required special educational courses before they could be usefully employed in the armed forces.
There should be a national interest in education generally because of the results shown by the Canadian provincial educational systems. When considered as a whole, looking at the broad picture, we find that over 50 per cent of Canadian children leave school before completing grade 8. This means that every other Canadian has had less than eight years of formal education. Yet the tendency is to require higher educational qualifications for admittance to many occupations. In other words we are denying to half our population an opportunity that should be their right through their childhood years; for the fact that so many do not complete their elementary education is due not so much to lack of interest on the part of the children, nor to lack of ambition for them on the part of their parents, as to lack of opportunity and lack of schools and trained teachers, or to unsatisfactory school conditions.
In the matter of denial of educational opportunity, I made an intensive investigation of that subject in the province of Manitoba about four years ago. I endeavoured to measure the standards of educational opportunity on the basis of the enrolment in the high schools. I found the average for the province showed that 18 per cent of the total number of children of school age were in high school. In the wealthier or more progressive areas, urban and rural, the percentage might rise to over 24 per cent, but in some areas of our province only 4 per cent of the children of school age were in high school. In these areas, for economic or other reasons, children discontinue school at grade 6 or grade 7 or grade 8, and do not receive the advantage of high school training. Either there are no high schools within reasonable distance of their homes, or the elementary schools have been so poorly organized or assisted that the children have not been successful in completing their courses. In some instances parental indifference may be the cause. Whatever the reason, this constitutes a denial of opportunity for many thousands of Manitoba children, and I imagine a similar survey in other provinces would indicate similar conditions.

Education
Basically the fault is economic. A great part of our trouble with education is primarily due to the lack of sufficient money to build and maintain schools and provide trained teachers. Very little is spent on the education of our children when you calculate the expenditure per child. For Manitoba, combining elementary and secondary schools and using the figures of the bureau of statistics for 1948, the average spent on each pupil was $157.27. I do not suppose there has been much change in the amount spent per pupil in the intervening years, but that amounted to less than 80 cents per pupil for each school day, the price of two packages of cigarettes. And for what? For daily instruction five times a week in the art of living and working together; in the study of the essential elements of education; in training for citizenship in a great democracy; in developing body, mind and character; in learning Canada's history and imbibing her traditions. No other task of comparable importance to the state is performed with such meagre support.
To the school taxpayer, the owner of real property, the cheapness of education is far from obvious. He finds it very burdensome, and cannot be blamed for urging that the weight on his shoulders be reduced. So long as the major cost of education is borne by a tax on land, our educational system will suffer from a lack of sufficient financial support. Other sources of revenue for education are urgently needed.
It is at this point that mention must be made of the Rowell-Sirois report, to which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) referred this afternoon. The able commissioners who surveyed the Canadian scene more than a decade ago hoped their recommendations for national adjustment grants would enable the provinces to maintain an average standard in all fields in which the provinces have jurisdiction. The hopes of the commissioners have not been realized. With regard to education the commissioners felt that they could not advise special grants for education in general. Again I quote the passage already quoted by the Minister of Justice:
Our financial proposals aim at placing every province in a position to discharge its responsibilities for education (on a scale that is within the means of the people of Canada) if it chooses to do so. Once this position is established it seems to us best that education like every other form of welfare service in a democratic community should have to fight for its life . . .
I end the quotation at that point because I take issue with the report there. Education, and certainly elementary education, should not have to fight for its life. Elementary education should be the right of our
fMr. Gauthier (Lake St. John).]
children, not a matter of choice for any governmental body. Similarly equal educational opportunity in secondary education and at the university level should be guaranteed every child in Canada. If any class or group in our society requires a bill of rights, it is the school age children of our country. Denial of educational opportunity is a blot upon the record of a country that so proudly points to its material achievements, its promising future and its heritage of freedom.
The answer lies in adequate financial support for education, with the federal authority providing the additional assistance that the provinces require. Slowly but steadily the federal government, through its extensive taxing powers and because of changing economic conditions, is becoming financially more powerful. The provinces, unless blessed with unusual natural resources, are unable to maintain from their restricted fields of direct taxation the services required. Some people consider that federal support for education means inevitably federal control or interference. Ottawa should not be allowed to grip any part of the provincial educational system.
There is already a considerable record of federal aid to education without federal control. The sum of $10 million was granted as early as 1913 to assist in agricultural training in the provinces. Other large sums have been made available for technical and vocational training, scholarships and for veterans training at the universities. Now we have an outright grant to universities. The federal government has established a pattern of assistance without control, and is showing am interest in education.
Education is of national concern and merits support from the federal treasury. Education is not just one among many competing welfare services. It is basic to the development of a democratic society. Education is a right which should not be denied any child in Canada. Opportunity for higher education should be the privilege of every Canadian boy and girl. A country composed of so many racial groups needs to place special emphasis on education in order to ensure the development of that unity within a federal system that is so essential for national development.
Further, I maintain that there is abundant proof that education still lacks sufficient financial support and that the only source from which the necessary assistance can be obtained is the federal treasury. Present interest by the federal authorities can be increased and present federal aid to education can be enlarged without curtailing provincial jurisdiction and responsibility.

The goal we seek is a united Canada. In the words of that great jurist, Mr. Justice Frankfurter of the United States:
The public school is at once the symbol of our democracy and the most pervasive means for promoting our common destiny.
By means of the schools of Canada we have the opportunity of maintaining our honoured traditions, of strengthening our democracy and of developing into greatness as a united nation.

Mr. Speaker, I have had the honour to represent the county of Dorchester in this house for 17 years. Needless to say I have heard speeches on many subjects, some timely, even urgent, some rather unimportant and some quite untimely. Since the beginning of the debate on this resolution, I have been wondering whether a certain group of members are not rather oblivious of the fact that the government of this country is based on a constitution which, if not very clear on certain matters, is very clear with regard to other subjects, particularly on the matter of jurisdiction in the field of education. The mover of this resolution apparently is asking for certain grants from the federal government!, This is precisely what we are opposing. The province of Quebec will never allow the federal government to encroach upon a field over which the province has complete jurisdiction.
The motion introduced by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada, by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose.
At this moment, Mr. Speaker, it would not be amiss perhaps to recall section 93 of the constitution which leaves no doubt whatever as to the jurisdiction in the field of education. Section 93 is entitled "Education" and reads as follows:
In and for each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to education, subject and according to the following provisions:
(1)	Nothing in any such law shall prejudicially affect any right or privilege with respect to denominational schools which any class of persons have by law in the province at the union;
(2)	All the powers, privileges, and duties at the union by law conferred and imposed in Upper Canada on the separate schools and school trustees of the queen's Roman Catholic subjects shall be and the same are hereby extended to the dissentient schools of the queen's Protestant and Roman Catholic subjects in Quebec.
Education
As I was saying, up to this point there is no ambiguity. Yesterday, the hon. members for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier), for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) and for Lake St. John (Mr. Gauthier)-I congratulate them all-clearly expressed in this house the reasons for our opposition to any interference on the part of the federal government in a field which comes under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. The hon. member for Portneuf had this to say in respect to the manner in which we deal, in the province of Quebec, with those of our fellow citizens whose tongue and religion are different from ours:
And now, Mr. Speaker, I feel Quebec has set an example with two councils of education, one for the Catholic schools, the other for Protestant or neutral schools. These two councils direct the policy of the provincial government in matters of education and keep the people of the province informed.
I shall go even further-here I call the attention of the hon. members from the other provinces, especially those who may be at the head of school boards-and state that the province of Quebec is setting an example which should be followed by all. In my province, grants are made without regard to the faith to which the educator belongs! Such an example is worth following.
Mr. Speaker, the sponsors of this motion seem entirely unaware that we are debating a question that is outside our scope. One thing is certain: whenever-be it today or at any other time in the future-a measure dealing with public education is brought before the house for approval, the province of Quebec will oppose it unanimously I am sure.
It is not my intention to stress the point at great length because it is self evident. No doubt about it, we are dealing with a matter outside our sphere of jurisdiction.
Some people may say "Haven't you stepped into that field already or do you believe that the granting of large subsidies to universities to further their development does not constitute intervention?"

I shall not go back to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, nor to Mr. Mackenzie King, and relate their achievements in that field, nor shall I recall everything the Liberal party has done in that connection; I shall merely give a quite recent illustration of the fact, an illustration which is still fresh in our minds. As far as the provincial field is concerned, I will be rather trite in asserting that, as Liberals, we must spend as much energy in order to safeguard provincial autonomy, as we do in defending the autonomy of Canada itself.
On November 22, 1949, the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent reminded Canadians, in a radio speech, of the following facts:
The British North America Act is Canada's constitution as well as the constitution of the provinces. 0
The Liberal party has always believed that the rights of the provinces must be respected and that no federal law can change, restrict or weaken the jurisdiction of the various provinces. In other words, it is essential to secure provincial co-operation . . .
The motion now before the house does not imply the co-operation of provincial authorities; it suggests, rather, that the federal government should intervene and distribute educational grants throughout Canada. That was not, however, our leader's opinion. He said:
In other words, provincial co-operation is essential to the institution of a complete and satisfactory method of amending our constitution.
A little further on in this speech which was listened to by almost everyone in this country, the Prime Minister added:
I could illustrate my point by comparing the constitution to a two-sided house of the type commonly known as a duplex, which is nothing more or less than a single house whose two sides are separated by one wall. Two families have been living in these two sides since 1867. But since that date, one family,-in this instance the provincial family,-could paper the walls, change the plumbing or even put in a new window without having to obtain permission from anybody, whereas the other family,-the federal family this time,- could not make such improvements without first getting permission from a landlord living in another country, some three thousand miles away. It must be added, however, that this landlord has always been very accommodating.

Well, we are of the opinion that both families should be able to decide by themselves what improvements they want to make to their own premises-and it is permission for the federal family to do so that we are asking, and nothing more.
We do not suggest that one of the two occupants should have the right to tear down the partition wall or to cut through the roof without consulting his neighbour. And that is why the representatives of the federal government and of the provincial governments will meet on January 10 next . . .
That was in January, 1950.
... in order to consult one another on the procedure to be followed if ever it becomes necessary to pull down the partition wall or repair the roof.
Well, I say that as Liberals it is our duty to be logical and to oppose the motion made by the hon. member for Saskatoon. I will not add anything further. If that motion is not untimely it is at least premature. If the provinces consider that their revenues do not allow them to give adequate assistance to education, let them come to an agreement with the federal government in order to obtain new sources of revenue, but as far as the federal government is concerned, "hands off" education.

I suppose that the tremendous interest in the financing of educational institutions at this time is due to the very large increase in the number of boys and girls who are now entering high school, compared with the number who entered forty or fifty years ago; and of these, the number who desire to go on to the universities. Consequently the methods of raising money for educational institutions that were quite satisfactory forty or fifty years ago are now not adequate.
I think we all agree that there must be no interference with the provincial control of education, but it seems to me the argument that the making of grants to our provinces for the purpose of education would be an interference is an argument that is not well founded, and, even after the minister's defence of it this afternoon, I still consider it to be ill-founded.
Our educational opportunities in this country are unevenly apportioned across the country. Some provinces may be well able to bear the expenditures that are necessary in connection with the modern educational system. Other provinces cannot bear the burden. As has already been said, if we are going to consider our country as a united nation, then every boy and girl in every part of Canada should have precisely the same opportunity for education as boys and
Education
girls that live in every other part of Canada. That is the reason why most of us are so anxious to see something done by the federal parliament to assist the provinces in the burden of education which they have to bear. And let us bear in mind that it is not only the provinces as provinces, but the municipalities themselves are unable, in the manner in which they have to raise the funds to carry on education, to do so adequately.
A great deal of criticism is made of the schools today. I have heard recent addresses in which it is said that the students entering our universities are not well equipped in the English language. After all, those of us who can look back forty or more years ago, when we were at high school or about to enter university, will remember that in those days we had none of those diversions we have today, neither the radio, the cinema nor the more modem thing, television. But we had good books. The result was that we read "The Pilgrim's Progress"; we read the Bible. When we were children we read G. A. Henty and W. H. G. Kingston, and the other stories that were told in good language. Today you have the newspapers with the comic strips and slang driven into the boys and girls every day of the year; consequently I say, Mr. Speaker, that anything we can do to promote a higher standard of education, particularly a higher standard of literature, whether it be the French language in Quebec or the English language in the English-speaking provinces, or both languages, which is better still, in all provinces of Canada, we should do it. We should do all that we can to achieve those desirable ends, but it will take still more and more financing, and the municipalities and the provinces cannot bear the burden. Mr. Speaker, I think we all agree that our human resources are the most valuable of all our resources and for that reason education is a matter of supreme and vital importance. We know also that some provinces have already reached the point where they can no longer

Education
cope with the tremendous problems of financing the education of children in the face of present costs. Furthermore, they see no hope of meeting the increasing demands of the foreseeable future without outside assistance. Of no province is this more true than of my own province of Newfoundland. No one would be happier than I to see some formula worked out whereby the federal government would share with the provinces the cost of educating our children, a burden which already is beyond the capacity of many provinces to bear.
I want to make it quite clear that I am not opposed to federal aid to education, but having said that I want to make it equally clear that I cannot support this resolution in its present form and I should like to place on record my reasons for not doing so. My first reason is that I do not know exactly what the resolution means, and I doubt if anyone else does. The key words are "equalizing educational opportunity." Before we can equalize anything we must have some standard by which to measure it and therefore we would need some standard that could be applied to educational opportunity in the various parts of Canada. Does such a standard exist? If it does, I have never heard of it and I doubt if any two educators in the world could agree on any such standard.
I should like to know exactly what is in the mind of my hon. friend who has introduced this resolution and of the hon. members who have supported it. Does he envisage selecting the standard of one province that has a very desirable system and bringing all other provinces up to that standard?
Does the hon. member wish me to answer that question?
Sit down.
I would rather finish.
I thought it was a question directed to myself.

You misunderstand
everything.

Does it mean that every person shall have an equal opportunity to the point of putting everyone through college? Does it mean that we will erect in every small village educational facilities similar to those to be found in the larger cities? I submit that equalization on that basis is a sheer impossibility.
If I were to select a standard of education for Canada I think I would select that of the province of Alberta. I have been greatly impressed by the educational work that has been done in Alberta. I have here a small pamphlet entitled "Quiet: Morals at Work"

published by the Lincoln Foundation at Louisville, Kentucky. It gives details of the work carried out by three teachers in Alberta, I believe in the city of Edmonton. I should like to bring this pamphlet to the attention of educators all across Canada.
When we start out to equalize educational opportunity across Canada who will be the judge? How shall we measure the equalization that we hope to accomplish? Then we have the words "educational opportunity." Exactly what do they mean? When introducing the resolution the hon. member placed on Hansard a table, to be found at page 591, giving the expenditure per pupil in the different provinces on elementary and secondary education, the expenditures on public, elementary and secondary education per pupil on an average daily attendance basis and on a per capita basis, and the median salaries of teachers in all schools. Does my hon. friend imply that educational opportunity is based on the per capita or per student expenditure? Anyone who has anything to do with education knows that money is but one factor, and a very small one, that goes to make up educational opportunity. An even more important factor than money is the teacher. Another important factor is that of home environment.
Then, along with these, there are other factors such as the curriculum, the system of education, educational administration, and even the objectives and values stressed in the curriculum, as well as the facilities for teaching, and the quality of teacher training. I do not think we should assume or be asked to infer, because one province spends three times as much per capita as another, or because the salaries are twice as great in one province as they are in another, that therefore the first province is supplying twice as much or three times as much educational opportunity as the second one.
As I said before, money is but one factor, and indeed one of the least important of the factors entering into educational opportunity. The expression "educational opportunity" is one that means different things to different people. It has various meanings in various parts of the country. I do not think we should vote for any resolution unless we know exactly what it means, and exactly what it is that we are voting for.
I note some hon. members have suggested the resolution simply means that the federal government should give out grants to the provinces for educational purposes, while other members have gone farther and said that these grants should be given without any strings attached. It is all very well for hon. members to make suggestions when they do not have to take the responsibility for results.
They are good at that.

The kind of assistance required to help the provinces meet their educational needs is going to run into hundreds of millions of dollars. The second question I would ask is this: where is this money to come from? If we take the total production in 1951 dollars and convert it to 1939 dollars, and divide that by the total man-hours worked, we find that our annual man-hour production has not increased very much over 1939. Unless we increase our annual man-hour production considerably we cannot find money from that source.
That leaves only two alternatives, one of which is a reduction of the present services, and the other increased taxation. Hon. members have not said what services they want reduced or what taxes they want increased. On the other hand they have charged this government with grossly overtaxing the people, and there is a general outcry for reduced taxation.
I cannot agree with hon. members who say that no strings should be attached to federal grants to provinces for education. It does not seem reasonable to me that the federal government should say to the provinces, "Here you are; we have got $20 million or $30 million for you. Take it and do what you like with it, so long as you spend it on education." I do not think that any responsible government conscious of its responsibilities to the taxpayers-and the taxpayers are the taxpayers of the provinces-could do such a thing.
Education is a very broad term; it is capable of many meanings; and it is quite possible that if money were granted on such a broad basis it could be used for purposes other than the purposes parliament might have in mind. And if such a thing should happen, then the very members who made this suggestion would turn round and charge the government with being grossly derelict in its duty, and guilty of gross neglect.
I do not see how any government can make grants of that magnitude-of the magnitude of hundreds of millions of dollars-without carefully prescribing the purposes for which the money is to be used, and the conditions under which it is to be expended. But the very minute the federal government does that it exposes itself to the charge of interfering with provincial rights.
The interests of the federal government should stem mainly from the national standpoint. I am not convinced that any province is doing all it can or should do to develop in our children a true appreciation of our national heritage or to develop the common loyalties and national thinking that are needed
Education
to make us a great nation. Instead of that we see some provinces indulging in what might be described as intellectual snobbery. Teachers who are highly qualified in one province are not qualified1 in another. We look across Canada from east to west and we see wide disagreement on educational aims, values and methods. We see that in one province grade 11 is the equivalent of grade 12 in another. We see wide differences in standards of curricula and of examinations.
No one would suggest that there should be a rigid system of education all across Canada, especially in a country as vast as ours. One of the functions of education is to be flexible so that it can meet the great variety of needs that arise in different places. But I still think that a far greater collaboration is possible than has been achieved at the present time; and a great deal more can be done to obtain uniformity of standards in the grading of pupils, in the grading of teachers, and in the awarding of diplomas.
It is my opinion that many provincial departments of education are too provincially minded. I doubt whether we should advocate that federal money should be spent to increase that tendency.
Another question I should like to have answered is this: even supposing we agree on a definition of educational opportunity, and even supposing we find a standard by which to measure it so that it may be equalized, on what basis would such grants be awarded? Would they be awarded purely on the basis of need, so that provinces which did not need money for education would not get any? Or would they be awarded on a per capita basis or per student basis? As soon as we do anything like that, Mr. Speaker, we create still further inequalities.
I do not think anyone can deny that a problem does exist, and it is a problem which in the national interest must be solved. If it is possible to find a formula under which the federal government can share the educational burdens of the provinces on particular items, such as teachers' salaries, classroom accommodation or teacher training, no one will be happier than I. Essentially, however, it is a provincial problem involving provincial rights, rights which are most jealously guarded. It has been pointed out on the floor of this house that already the federal government is providing assistance in as many ways and to as great an extent as the British North America Act will permit. That assistance has been estimated to amount to some $35 million. Therefore I think it would be not only unwise but highly improper for the federal government to take any initiative

Education
in matters pertaining to primary education in Canada, which is essentially a provincial responsibility. Because it is a provincial responsibility, I feel that the initiative should come from the provinces, not from this government. For that reason I aim not able to support this resolution.

I think it is an excellent thing, Mr. Speaker, that the members of this house should have the opportunity to debate in detail this very important subject of education. Just two weeks ago we as a nation observed education week. For several years the slogan that has been adopted in connection with that week is this very appropriate phrase: "Education is everybody's business". That being so, I think we as members of this house can take it upon ourselves from time to time to give consideration to the situation concerning education in this country.
Tonight I do not want to go into the constitutional aspects of the problem. Neither do I want to deal with the question of standardization, which was raised by the previous speaker, mainly because I do not think the resolution as it stands carries any implication concerning standardization. It refers to equalization of educational opportunities across Canada. During the few minutes I am going to speak this evening I want to view the problem from the standpoint of one who has recently come from the educational field. As a matter of fact I might style myself as one who started on the road to Damascus and fell among politicians. Whether or not that was a good thing remains to be seen.
Some people seem to have the impression that the controversy or discussion today concerning educational matters is a case of crying wolf, that actually the field of education is not as badly off as this discussion would indicate. I think we must admit that the interest which has been aroused in educational matters during the past few years would indicate that there is a real crisis, a real problem to be dealt with. For example, an article in the Canadian Home Journal by Hugh MacLennan, one of our outstanding Canadian writers and novelists, described teaching as the thankless profession. In his opening paragraph he said:
The most exploited, neglected and underprivileged class in Canada are not people the comfortable classes never see. They are not sharecroppers, migrant fruit pickers, sweat shop girls, or fishermen in outposts. They are the nation's school teachers.
That was Mr. MacLennan's description of the situation, in 1949. I believe it was H. G. Wells who said that civilization is a race between education and catastrophe. He may

have exaggerated a little; but the way governments have been studying the problem and the interest educationists have been showing in recent years would indicate that something is seriously wrong with our educational system. I might mention several reports, including the famous report of the Harvard commission on education. In Manitoba in the years following the war we had several surveys of our educational problems, and the provincial government has put out two different reports on educational matters, one on general education and the other on adult education.
Regardless of the constitutional difficulties, regardless of the splitting of hairs as far as this resolution is concerned I think it would be a tragedy if we should permit institutional and political rigidity to prevent us from facing the realities of the problem. There was a time when a study of the three R's would be sufficient for the ordinary citizen, the famous "readin', writin', 'rithmetic, taught to the tune of the hickory stick". From the remarks of one speaker this afternoon I gained the impression that he was harking back to the days of the three R's, when he referred to some of the unnecessary frills in the educational system at present, particularly in Ontario. I would suggest that some of these things we are prone to call frills today are really necessities.
As the previous speaker indicated, schools are not the only source of education. There are all kinds of informal sources of education, such as the press, radio, television, the cinema and even the books which are being banned from the stands in the city of Ottawa. They are all informal sources of education. Then there is the family and the church. I would like to point out that one reason for the crisis in education at the present time arises from the fact that the family and the church are not performing the functions they formerly performed. Owing to social change, owing to industrialization, urbanization and so forth, we find that some of the functions which formerly belonged to these other social institutions have now fallen upon our schools. And in assuming these new responsibilities our schools find that the problem of producing educated, mature citizens to meet the challenge of living in a very complex world is a much more expensive proposition than it was in the days of the little red school house and the basic three R's.
An indication that we are facing problems in that regard is seen in the rise of various new professions trying to fill the social vacuum. We have social workers of various kinds who are trying to mend the pieces

of our society, trying to catch the victims of this complex civilization when they reach the bottom of the hill, instead of putting a fence at the top of the hill to prevent the casualties. We have psychiatrists. We have marriage counsellors, endeavouring to deal with an increasing problem of family breakdowns and divorce. Those people are very important in the kind of society we have; but I would suggest that of all these social welfare people the most important is this neglected individual to whom Hugh Mac-Lennan referred in his article as the most neglected and underprivileged in Canada.
In referring to social workers, we sometimes use the term "social engineer." If we are justified in using that term, I think the school teacher is the "social engineer" par excellence, in the type of society in which we live today. Compare the training of a teacher and a teacher's salary with the sort of training that goes into the preparation of professional people in other walks of life such as the legal profession, dental or medical profession or an engineer. This reveals that the standards we have for these important people, the school teachers, are ridiculous. Before a dentist can pull teeth, he has to have at least five years at university. A doctor has to have six or seven years at university, while an engineer has to have four or five years before he can build roads or bridges. The school teacher, who carries the large load of equipping our young people to live in this world today, does not have to meet such rigorous standards. We all know that schools are carrying on almost a cradle to the grave program today, with adult education, kindergartens and so forth. We all know, too, that there is a tendency for parents to bring their youngsters to the doorstep of the school almost as soon as they can toddle and say, "Here they are, learn 'em good." That is all the parents see of them until they graduate at the end of the assembly line.
These professional people, the teachers who are entrusted with the task of working with human personalities-with human souls if you will-well, any sort of training will do. I do not thinJk there is any question of equality of opportunity under those circumstances. In Manitoba, for example, we have over 500 permit teachers. A permit teacher tends to be a grade 11 student who has flunked too many subjects to go on to grade 12, so he goes into the rural areas to be a teacher. In Manitoba we still have over 500 of them entrusted with this very important task of producing mature, democratic citizens in the sort of world we have to face at the present time. Some say, and this is an argument that harks back to the three
Education
R's tradition, that you do not need much education to teach kindergarten children. I would say here is where the basic job of education is done. Unfortunately, we get the poorest teachers in the kindergarten because they are paid the lowest salaries. These low paid permit teachers gravitate to the important job of introducing youngsters to their first experience in the schoolroom.
Fortunately, we are getting the single salary schedule in some places. Wherever teachers have equal qualifications, regardless of whether those qualifications are used in elementary, high school or university, they are recognized by an equal salary. The reason that cannot be done on a comprehensive scale is due to the financial problem which has been dealt with during this debate today.
In addition to the teacher problem, there is the matter of facilities. We have the one-room rural school in which the teacher conducts nine grades. Such facilities are hardly adequate to give a child the necessary educational background today. We have the large school area that is being developed in the rural parts of the country in order to overcome the handicap of inadequate facilities. In Manitoba this idea has been promoted since the end of the war, but the results have not been very successful so far. We have only one large school area. The other main problem of education, that is the curriculum, is automatically overcome when we have a large school area because then you can give the broad curriculum that is necessary to meet the diversified needs of the young people in our society. In the prairie provinces -it is a little different in provinces like Ontario and Quebec-the high school program is largely based on the theory that most of the students are going on to college. They are all given a broad general academic training. In reality, only two or three per cent of the high school graduates continue on to university and into the professions. You have, therefore, a completely unrealistic approach to the problem. The commercial areas, business, technology, agriculture and so forth, are completely neglected so far as school programs are concerned.
This inequality of opportunity that is mentioned in the resolution is most noticeable in the rural areas. It is quite obvious that the rural part of the country does not offer the same opportunities as the urban areas. In fact, the school systems in the larger cities are in excellent shape so far as qualified teaching personnel, physical facilities and curriculum are concerned. These provisions are made at the expense of exorbitant municipal taxation. If we need to have

Education
emphasized any more than has been emphasized the problem of inequality in educational opportunity, we need only refer to the discrimination that exists between rural and urban students. With rural-urban migration going on as it is today, the rural student is placed at a decided disadvantage.
We have had it pointed out that lack of funds is at the root of the matter. Some hon. members have attempted to demonstrate that the provinces have sufficient resources at the present time to bring educational standards up to the level required. One member from Ontario held out a great promise for the prairie provinces by saying that we are just becoming industrialized. If we are only patient, we shall soon have enough money to bring up the standard of education to equal that of any province.
But at the rate of industrialization going on in Manitoba at the present time, particularly in regard to defence industry, I cannot see much hope for a solution to this problem in the next few years. We are actually faced with a crisis to such an extent that Mr. MacLennan, to quote him again in that article, says:
Our whole system of popular education is in danger of disintegration . . . and that means ruin for a whole society.
Let me stress again that is not merely crying "havoc" or merely crying "wolf". Those who are closely associated or who have been closely connected with the problems of education today are greatly disturbed at the inadequacies and inefficiencies. As to where the solution lies, I do not know. I am not going to attempt to offer any solution tonight. I am not going to attempt to outline a master plan. But at the root of the matter, I repeat, is the lack of sufficient funds. Federal aid could assist in that matter, or maybe provincial aid, provided that the provinces had sufficient revenue to meet the extremely high costs of adequate education at the present time.
In view of the importance of our human resources, I think something should be done. I could give all sorts of concrete examples of young people in our part of the world who have been deprived of an adequate opportunity because of inadequate schooling facilities. I think it is imperative that, above all else, we preserve our human resources. I do not think anyone will disagree with the expression of opinion that there is not the proper emphasis on our educational system at the present time. If we compare the money we spend on other things-and I need only mention, as an example, the money that is poured into liquor, and the profits accruing therefrom-that comparison in itself would

indicate that there is a real basic need to heal the schism in the body politic. When thousands-yes, millions-of people can stand to look at the world only through an alcoholic haze, there must be something wrong with the sort of world they are living in.
I would suggest again that when teachers get together and discuss these problems they are not just talking through their hats. They are talking because they see a real situation, a real need, a real problem; and I maintain that it is one of the basic problems we have to solve at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, the motion before the house reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada, by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose.
Mr. Speaker, may I submit what I consider to be the views of the province of Quebec in the matter. In my province we do not want any federal grants for education. I was quite surprised, today, to see how the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) and members of his group and the C.C.F. group endeavoured to force upon the province of Quebec something which we do not want. We have reasons of our own to oppose this procedure. We want to maintain the principle which is recognized under our constitution. As a matter of fact the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) clearly indicated in a brilliant and sincere speech this afternoon that the province of Quebec was justly opposed to federal interference in the field of education, because, as I said, of the very special nature of the problem of education in our province.
We have tried to develop French culture in the province of Quebec, and that culture, thanks to our institutions of learning, has extended beyond our boundaries. But we want this culture to develop throughout this country from sea to sea, concurrently with Anglo-Saxon culture. I believe this will be one of the best ways to ensure, in our country, that national unity we all long for.
Mr. Speaker, the leader of the opposition endeavoured to prove this afternoon that the province of Quebec should receive those grants the same as all the other provinces. I listened to him without surprise. I am convinced that the Conservative party is prompted by the bureaucrats who direct our public service and

whose sole aim is to centralize the whole state apparatus under the control of Ottawa. As I have just said, I am by no means surprised that the members of the C.C.F. party should want to place our whole educational system under federal control in order to weld together the two cultures which up to now have developed along parallel lines, but on which rest the richness and strength of our national unity.
I know that certain members of our federal bureaucracy, whom the influence of the French language annoys, are constantly urging the members of the two political groups in front of us to do what they can to lessen the prestige of our beautiful idiom. May I be permitted to quote the poet's verses on the French language:
To try to stop Its flight is to try to keep buds and roses from blooming:
To try to destroy its power and its charm is to dream of preventing the appearance of the dawn.
You cannot do it, gentlemen. Your efforts are useless. Let me say to the leader of the opposition and to the leader of the C.C.F. party that their attempts are doomed to failure because the province of Quebec knows that the acceptance of grants results in subservience.
During the provincial election in Quebec, the Hon. Mr. Duplessis advocated absolute refusal of any grant from the federal government for purposes of education. I repeat here the words he used at all his meetings. Recently, he accepted a sum of money given to him as the result of one of the recommendations of the Massey report. I therefore say that he has capitulated for he accepted, from the federal government, money that only a few months ago he spurned with horror. The province of Quebec will keep that in mind at the next provincial election and will ask him what happened to his campaign in favour of autonomy in the field of education, which besides was a farce, as is now the stand taken by the Progressive Conservative party. I do not mention the C.C.F. for their very doctrine is based on centralization, but at least they say so frankly. The Progressive Conservative party, through its leader's utterances, has gone on record as being in full accord with this proposal, put forward by a party fundamentally committed to centralization.
The Hon. Mr. Duplessis, it seems to me, had he wished to use the revenues of the province of Quebec, could have found all the money necessary to further the cause of education in our province, through the provision of generous grants. The federal government offered him the use of five per cent of the income tax paid in by every individual.
Education
In other words, out of every hundred dollars paid in by the taxpayer to the Department of National Revenue, the province, according to the terms offered by the federal government, would have received five dollars, without having to disburse one cent. As a matter of fact, such a proposal was made by the chambers of commerce of the province of Quebec in order to assist education. He could thus have given our universities about $8 million. The Hon. Mr. Duplessis saw fit to ignore this generous offer and now he is accepting the federal government's grants.
Thus we see that the position of the leader of the opposition here in Ottawa, in so far as grants to the provinces for purposes of education are concerned, is identical to that presently being adopted by the Hon. Mr. Duplessis.
The leader of the opposition wants the federal government to subsidize education in the provinces. We are against it. Such is the attitude of the province of Quebec. Gentlemen, at the next federal election, we will remind you of the position the Progressive Conservative party has just taken. We will also remind the Hon. Mr. Duplessis of his recent capitulation in accepting grants he had formerly denounced.

I am not going to attempt to follow the hon. member who has just taken his seat, either in form, eloquence or vigour. I think the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) deserves credit for again bringing this resolution before the house. It is an important resolution. The question of equalization of education in this dominion is one which concerns a great many people. It is not my intention to take very much time this evening. I followed the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) this afternoon. He pointed out a fact which we all know, that, as far as administration is concerned, education is something which is entirely under the jurisdiction of the province. No one in this house, and I am sure no one in this country, wants to change that fact.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat spoke eloquently of the loss of autonomy in the province of Quebec if the federal government should give grants for education.
I am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that neither the province of Quebec, the province of Ontario, nor any other province in Canada would lose one iota of its autonomy if a grant were made to the different provinces for education. As a matter of fact, in speaking this afternoon the minister said that if a grant of money were made for education the federal government would have to exercise some care, or some supervision, over the spending of that

Education
money in the different provinces. That does not follow at all, Mr. Speaker. We all know that at the present time, in grants and subsidies, the federal government is paying out millions of dollars to the different provinces of this country. I should like to ask any member of the government whether they are supervising the money which is being spent now in the provinces, or which is being given to the provinces in these large grants and subsidies? In some few instances they are, but the great bulk of this money is under the administration of the provinces and the federal government is exercising no influence over the expenditure of that money, nor would they exercise any influence over money which might be granted to the provinces for education.
The minister also said that it is within the purview of the provincial governments to spend their money as they wish. He asked: Why not spend it for education, if it is necessary, and not spend it for public works or for some other service? Down in my province, Mr. Speaker, if we spent less money than we do for public works, or for some other services, we would not have any roads or we would not have those public services. An argument of that kind does not sound good in a debate such as this.
We do need help. We do need help in the smaller provinces in this Dominion of Canada. We need help in New Brunswick. They need help in Newfoundland, despite the argument of the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) a few moments ago. A province that pays only $900 average to its teachers needs help, and no member from that province need stand in his place in this house and tell us that under such circumstances they do not need more assistance than they get from their own government.
As I say, we in New Brunswick need this assistance. They need it in all the four small provinces down by the sea. They may not need it in Ontario-I do not believe they do. Ontario is a very wealthy province. I do not think they need it in Quebec. Quebec is a wealthy province. It is not needed so much in the province of Alberta, which is becoming a very wealthy province. That also applies to the province of British Columbia, which can afford to pay some $2,500 or $2,600 to its teachers. But we need it, Mr. Speaker. I believe the time will come, whether it is done by this government or by some other government, when assistance will have to be given to these small provinces to carry on education.
I want to correct the impression which I think some hon. members gave to the house,

and this is one of my chief reasons for rising to speak. In the different tables that were presented yesterday afternoon and in the comparison given of the number of pupils who leave school under grade 8, it was stated that 58 per cent of the pupils of the province of New Brunswick leave school before they finish grade 8. We have in New Brunswick a system which is different from those in most other provinces. We have graded schools, and ungraded schools. The small schools in the country districts are ungraded schools; they do not run up to grade 8. But, as a matter of fact, the pupil who graduates from a country school has the equivalent education of grade 8 or even a higher grade, so when they say that 58 per cent of the pupils of New Brunswick never reach grade 8, that is a mistake or misinformation.
In our province, under a great burden, we have also been endeavouring to increase our school facilities. In our province we have been very proud of our schools. As I pointed out when speaking on this resolution in a former year, when South Africa wanted a system of education for that dominion they came to the province of New Brunswick and selected the system which we then had in our province. We are not as backward in education as perhaps some people might think after listening to the addresses in this house. What we need is money, and more money in order to provide the educational facilities needed by our children.
There is another argument that could be advanced, a very practical one. Last year New Brunswick imposed a 4 per cent sales tax because its resources were not sufficient to provide the revenue for education. That sales tax was in addition to the sales tax imposed by the dominion and it represents a tremendous burden. An extra 4 per cent must be paid on everything the people buy, which, I repeat, is a tremendous burden for our small province to bear.
One hon. member said that education should be of great concern to the federal government, but he pointed out also that that government is now giving considerable aid to education by its support of the Royal Military College, vocational grants, education grants, education of Indians and so on. Another hon. member pointed out that education in connection with national defence should be of great concern to the federal government. I think it was the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) who made that statement, and I agree with him. During the last war I was in charge of a military training centre and I was amazed at the number of young men coming up for recruitment who had to be turned

down because they did not have the necessary educational qualifications. It seemed to me to be a great loss as far as military training was concerned.
I do not want to take up too much time because I should like to see this matter come to a vote tonight. Before closing, I should like to mention one native of New Brunswick, a man who was born and educated in that province, who left it and then came back and has contributed greatly to education in our province. I refer to Lord Beaverbrook. He has furnished many scholarships for training in universities in Canada and in Europe, particularly in England. We are most grateful to him for the assistance he has given.
I do not think it is necessary for me to labour this point any further. The province of New Brunswick needs assistance, and needs it badly. I know that the province of Nova Scotia needs assistance. When the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) spoke on this matter last year he mentioned that fact. The hon. member regrets that for business reasons he is unable to be here this evening. The need is there as the smaller provinces want to have opportunities equal to those possessed by the richer provinces. The only way to my mind that that can be done is by some assistance from the federal government.
I do not think it is necessary for the federal government to supervise the money given for educational purposes. Surely the men who represent the people in the different provinces are responsible enough to spend that money in the best interests of the children of their provinces. I think the argument advanced by the minister falls absolutely flat. I am satisfied that money can be granted to the provinces without their losing one iota of their autonomy, as one hon. member from Quebec is afraid would happen.

Mr. Speaker, I take part in this debate on the invitation of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) who said that no Liberal member from Saskatchewan had expressed his views on this matter. I have no hesitation in expressing mine. I would refer to a previous debate when the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. Smith) said that if these gentlemen want to debate in a rather lively manner, we are the boys to do it. I join this debate on those terms.
The premise of the argument advanced by the hon. member in support of his motion seems to be equality of educational opportunity for children across the land. Those hon. members who come from Saskatchewan will remember that that was the slogan of the C.C.F. when they came into power in 55704-41$
Education
that province in 1944. They were going to provide equality of education in Saskatchewan. How far have they come along that road? One thousand schools have been closed since these gentlemen took over and we now have study supervisors in charge of 558 of those schools. They are known in Saskatchewan as sitters. They perform the duty that you would naturally think a sitter would perform: they sit. They try to keep a little order in the schoolroom. Some of them are high school pupils and have some teaching ability and they try to carry on some of the work of instruction. But it does not matter what line of business you are in, if you have no qualifications you cannot carry it on as successfully, and that applies to sitters.
It has been suggested by this motion that the federal government should grant the provinces assistance for educational purposes. I disagree with the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) because I do not think you can hand over money to the provinces for education willy-nilly. If we did that to any great extent there would not be any need for any of us being here. The federal government would just be a taxation collection agency to turn the money over to the provinces to be spent in the way they wanted to spend it.
That is not my idea of the function of the dominion government. We must have some supervision over how money is spent if we are going to take money from the taxpayer. Hon. members of the opposition have never been backward in giving away money as long as it is somebody else's. They are not too concerned about how it is spent.
The minister of finance in Saskatchewan has just brought down his budget and I should like to draw attention to his educational program. The receipts under revenue account total $1,681,920. I can break down that figure if necessary. Then there are receipts from the education and hospital tax which is a sales tax. When these gentlemen came into power and said that they were going to have equality of education, they said also they were going to take off this tax. Instead they have increased it 50 per cent. It is now called an education and hospital tax, one-third being used for hospitalization and two-thirds for education. Allowing for the cost of administration, the net amount for education is $7,231,020.
Then there is the public revenue tax which is collected by the municipalities. This was originally earmarked for road work in the municipalities, but it has now been taken over by the provincial government and they are going to throw that into the education tax pot. Off this $1,600,000 you take $80,000 for commissions for collection, leaving you

Education
a net from your public revenue of $1,520,000. The total receipts earmarked for educational account are therefore $10,432,940. The estimated payments on educational account, according to Mr. Fines, the minister of finance out there, show expenditures of $11,708,600. Therefore, deducting those two totals you find that from special taxation in the province for education, or from receipts from outside sources-from the federal government in some instances, in connection with schools for the deaf and so on-you have a discrepancy there the province will have to pay of $1,275,660. Thus $1,275,660 is all it is costing them for education in that province, outside of what they have from special taxes.
Where do they stand in their revenues? This year they are getting from the federal government-and they say they should be getting more-some $26 million. In 1939 that was something over $2 million. So their revenues have gone up, in spite of the federal government. What are the other expenditures they may have out there? Well, according to the minister of finance in the province, here is what is being spent on social service and health-and we are interested in that, if we are going to give money to the province. I am interested to know what they are doing with what they have now. Altogether, social welfare is costing something more than $10 million and public health $18 million, making a total of $28,560,000. Then, less the federal government account for public health and social welfare amounting to $2,568,000, along with some other deductions, they are left a net of $25,062,000. They take off the one-third of their educational tax which goes for hospitalization-a direct tax for that purpose-which gives the sum of $3,615,000, and we find that they are spending on social services, altogether, the sum of $21,447,000 or, in other words, about twenty-one and a half million.
The net cost of public health is therefore about $21,500,000 and the net cost of education is about one and a quarter million. The total cost of both public health, social aid and education in the province is $22,722,850.
Their subsidies from the federal government this year amount to $26,727,520, leaving them a net over income from the federal government of $5,280,330. In other words the federal government pays for all the social aid, it pays for all the education and it pays for all the public health in the province of Saskatchewan. And they still have $5,280,000 left.

There is no reason why they could not apply some of that to education. We do not say how they have to use it. And I thought the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) put it very squarely this afternoon, for anyone who wishes to read his speech. However, this is what we are doing with our money in Saskatchewan, under the government we have out there now. Certainly I do not think anyone would want to hand out a lot more money to be handled in that way. If we are going to have a thousand schools closed at the end of that time, and another 558 with sitters, then we see there the worst situation in education to be found anywhere in Canada. When there is an effect there is always a cause. What is the cause of our not having teachers? Well, we have there a government with a mania for control and regimentation. We have there a government that insists upon price controls, and that enters very closely into this picture. It used to be that the local school board, if it wanted to hire a teacher, found out how much the teacher was worth on the market, looked over their assessment in that district and decided whether they could pay that much money, whether they would have the teacher or would not. Under those circumstances we always had teachers.
Now, however, we do not have teachers for the simple reason that our government has said that the larger school units will do the hiring, and they do not go into the competitive market. They take the competition right out of it.
You do not believe that, yourself.

These gentlemen do not
believe in competition. They do not believe in free trade in teachers, or anything else. So that is why we have no teachers-for the simple reason that the local school boards cannot go out and hire teachers, even if they want to. They have to sit back and take what they get-and they get 558 sitters.

Whom are you fooling,
Jack?

The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight), having invited me into this dance, naturally will expect me to kick the furniture around. He says that 90 per cent of the people in the ridings represented by Liberal members from Saskatchewan are behind federal aid for education. Well, I was home in January, and I think I spent as much time on the road as did the next man. As a matter of fact I travelled something over 5,000 miles while I was there, and was away from home practically every

day. I can say that I never had anyone mention to me, federal aid for education. I did have a lot of them mention the fact that there was no education, that they were not getting any. In fact, one gentleman told me that his child had been in school for six years and had never yet had a teacher. He had had nothing but sitters. Fortunately he had had a couple of good sitters, and he said he learned many things from them.
However, I do not think that the mere handing of more money to these gentlemen will improve the situation at all, if they are still unwilling to let the school boards go out and hire teachers for what those teachers are worth.
Another contribution they made to education was to close the normal school at Regina. Well, how are we going to have teachers if we close the normal schools? Very few youngsters will want to take training as teachers when the only future they have ahead of them is that of sitting.
If we give money to a government that has shown itself as irresponsible as the one in Saskatchewan, will that get more education? And then the question arises that one might be educated and still have no wisdom. That does not help, either.
That applies to you in this instance.

Thank you, sir. As I said, after the federal government pays for all the social services in the province, and pays their health bill, and all sorts of services for education, they have $5 million left from what they receive from the federal government. What do they do with that amount of money? Well, they go out and build theatres under the stars. We have open air theatres at Weyburn built with government money that could have been used for education. Is that an indication that we should hand more money over to these gentlemen just to throw around? They might even give it to Mr. Schumiatcher, and he would get a commission for advising them to give it to him.
I make these remarks to show mainly that, in a mild way, I am opposed to this resolution.

The hon. member for Saskatoon has said that 90 per cent of the people who are supposed to be interested in federal aid for education are to be found m Liberal ridings in Saskatchewan. Again, as I said, I have not found any of them who

were interested enough to mention it to me. Some of them did complain about there being no education.
