Mr. Speaker, I rise purely for the purpose of setting the record straight on one point. I listened with great regret this evening to the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix) who, if I understood him correctly, spent a good deal of time in suggesting that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) had used language inconsistent with the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces over education. That was my understanding of what the hon. member said, with great vehemence. I want to point out that that was an absolute travesty; not only a travesty but an absolute contradiction of clear language used yesterday by the leader of the opposition. I want to put on the record very briefly what the leader of the opposition said on this point, to show how utterly inconsistent it is with the suggestion of the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency. At page 608 of Hansard, after discussing the question in general terms, the leader of the opposition said:
That being the situation, confronted with the necessity for dealing with this subject in a manner that will equalize the opportunity for education right across Canada today, what can be done to meet this situation without in any way impairing the constitutional position and the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial governments over education? That is the question that we must be able to answer if we are, in turn, to indicate any way in which the government, with the support of the parliament of Canada, can tackle this problem.
I submit nothing could be clearer, more unambiguous or positive, and I again express my regret that the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency should have so distorted-I think that is a fair word-what was said. As I stated in rising, I wished to put the record straight during this sitting of the house so there could be no misunderstanding whatever.

Mr. Speaker, my main reason for participating in this debate is to take this first opportunity to repudiate and refute if possible a statement made during the course of this debate yesterday afternoon. At the time the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) was speaking, and at page 594 of Hansard, he said:
If a boy or girl is too lazy to study, no grant from the government of Canada will change his or her mind. In the first place, with regard to education, there must be on the part of every student the determination and will to learn something. In the

Education
second place there must be on the part of the teacher the ability to make something understood by the student. The thing works both ways.
The hon. member lor York South (Mr. Noseworthy) then interjected:

Education
many of the difficult social and educational problems America has come to face are national in scope and character and call for general and country-wide solution.
May I draw the attention of the house to the last sentence which reads as follows:
To assist in such national solution many nationwide agencies have been set up, and there has been a strong and persistent movement for some national financial aid to the states, and for a secretary of education in the president's cabinet.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member should give the number of the page and the volume from which he is quoting.

That is the 1949 edition of the Encyclopedia Britannica, volume 7, page 996, the first column, and the closing paragraph. You will note, Mr. Speaker, that in the United States, together with the desire for some financial aid to the states from the national authority, and tied in with it in the same sentence, is the statement that there is also a body of opinion favouring a secretary of education in the president's cabinet, a department of education at the national level.
That, Mr. Speaker, is a preview of the problem which faces us today.

Mr. Speaker, I have but a few words to say. I am not here for the purpose of contributing in any way to talking this resolution out. All I want to do is to voice my support for it, as I have done on previous occasions, and to say that in so far as the Progressive Conservative party is concerned, the attitude that we take is that, constitutionally, education is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces and shall remain so; and that any contribution made in order to carry out the purpose of this resolution, namely to take into consideration means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity, in no way implies control. Simply paraphrasing a slogan of another day, the attitude of this party is: Federal assistance ever; federal supervision never. That sums up our attitude on this matter.
I know that the members in all parts of the house wish to have the opportunity of standing up on this occasion and being counted. Having expressed my approval of the resolution, I therefore take my seat.

Mr. Speaker, it was my intention to say a few words on this resolution when it was before the house last year, but I was prevented from doing so. This year, particularly in view of the many interpretations that have

been placed on the resolution, I therefore felt that I could not reasonably vote on it without stating my position.
A great many statements have been made on education generally; that is, on education in general without particular regard to the resolution. In this respect the resolution will have some merit and make some contribution to a consideration of the question as a whole. I think it is a good thing that the Canadian people as a whole should be seized with the importance of this problem of education in this country at the present time. With most of these general considerations, I think all hon. members of the house are agreed. I am sure that we all want improvement, as for that matter do all people throughout the country.
Nobody will quarrel with the idea that we should have better schools. By that I mean better buildings to house the children. From travelling around our respective provinces and throughout the country we all know that there is great need for improved facilities in a great many parts of Canada. I suppose that this condition will be with us for quite some time because there will always be room for improvement. But in connection with this whole question, there is another significant point that arrests our attention throughout the country today, namely the need for a more competent staff to teach the children in the schools. The figures have already been placed on the record by more than one speaker, and I do not intend to repeat them. With such a large number of teachers teaching on permits only, it is obvious that this situation could be a threat to education as a whole. After all, all those who are teaching on permits at the present time are people who have not been trained to do this highly specialized and technical job.
With that problem I suppose we could couple the problem that arises out of the present pay that teachers are receiving. Those figures have also been placed on the record by a great many members, and I do not intend to do it now. From the smallness of the pay that the educators of the nation are receiving at the present time, it is obvious that they would naturally be attracted into other fields than that of education. Unless this situation is remedied, I am afraid the trend will be for the situation to continue to get worse instead of better.
This resolution also brings forward something else and that is, if I might term it so, the suggestion for more education for the children of Canada; by that I mean a higher standard of education and with that a better opportunity or more equal opportunity for

all the children of the nation. With regard to those last two points, I feel strongly that there is definitely room for improvement. In many parts of this country it is not easy for a young man even to go through the primary and secondary schools to get a higher education without financial means of some sort. There are many countries in the world where children can get a higher education and can complete their education in much easier ways than we have available in this country. I think it is obvious that there is room for a good deal of improvement in these various lines. As it now reads, I feel that this resolution is hardly compatible with provincial autonomy in education; and I propose to elaborate a little on that point. But this general discussion on federal aid to education is, I believe, at the present time having some adverse effect in the nation. So much has been said about federal aid to education -the term has been used very loosely, almost everybody has a different concept and a different meaning for it-that it seems to have been accepted in a great many parts of the nation, or among the public generally, as a cure-all of all the shortcomings of our educational system in Canada. It seems to have been accepted as a cure-all formula; it seems to have been accepted as a system that would cure the shortcomings of our educational system in each province without any effort in particular by anybody. It has, in this respect, distracted attention away from the authorities who really have the responsibility in this matter and have the power to remedy the situation. Therefore I think it would be well to place it in its proper perspective and apply the resources, if I may say so, of everybody concerned, who wants a better educational system in Canada, where they will do the most good and where the authority lies to improve the condition.
For instance, in this debate we have seen that some speakers have looked upon this .resolution as meaning a grant to either vocational schools or universities. In the minds of many in the country, federal aid to education means grants to universities, and on that basis they agree wholeheartedly with the resolution. However, some others believe this resolution means grants to primary and secondary education. There again some people agree with this suggestion; but a great many people do not agree with the suggestion that the federal government should make grants to primary and secondary education. Therefore there are many concepts of federal aid to education.
Education
Yesterday and today we have seen another version, another interpretation of this resolution by the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Drew). According to his remarks it would appear that he looks upon this resolution, or the interpretation he places upon it, as merely an expansion of the tax fields. According to him this resolution means that it is simply giving the provinces a greater opportunity of levying taxes. I must confess that upon reading the resolution over and over again I cannot see that it means just that, and the impression I got from the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) on every occasion that he has spoken on his resolution is that it was definitely aid or assistance or grants to all levels of education. At least he never voiced any objections to grants or assistance to any level of education in particular. If the resolution actually means only that we are considering giving another field for the provinces in which they can raise money, then on that basis I would assume that almost any hon. member would be quite free to support it. But the way the resolution reads it states specifically:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada-
Then it goes on to state the way in which it should be done namely:
-by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose.
I do not think there is any way out of it; it definitely means to earmark grants to the provinces for that purpose. Therefore the general interpretation that has been placed upon it by the official opposition is not in accordance with the resolution. I do not think it can be so interpreted and agree with the wording of the resolution.
In the discussion so far everybody has proceeded from the basis that education was the primary responsibility of the provinces. All those who have spoken so far in the house have advocated that provincial autonomy should be maintained as such. This afternoon the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) made the statement that he did not know of any resolution that had received as much general support as this one. These are not his exact words, but that is the idea they conveyed. In some respects I suppose it could be true; but as I said, when you consider the interpretation that has been placed upon it by a great many people, you will find that a great many of them support it, and at the same time support a different thing altogether. Therefore it is very hard to
650

Education
determine who supports what in this resolution, unless we define our terms and define what we mean by federal aid to education.
The feeling that is abroad, that if the federal government will take it over it will relieve municipalities of a heavy burden, is, in many instances, basically the idea that it would leave them more revenues to spend on something else. In many quarters nowadays they do not even stop to try to distinguish between federal aid through provincial autonomy and federal aid generally. I was very much surprised to get a resolution from the Manitoba Associated Chambers of Commerce. They passed a resolution at their 21st annual convention on December 5 and 6. Their resolution would indicate that they consider the time has arrived for the federal government to take over the responsibility of education in Canada. In all fairness to them I think I should place the whole resolution on the record. It is headed: "Dominion Aid to Education", and reads as follows:
Whereas the subject of education in recent years has become one of the most important governmental problems and has now emerged as a social problem of equal status with old age security, pensions and unemployment insurance; and
Whereas the growing girl and boy represent the citizens of democracy of the future and constitute Canada's greatest investment for the future; and
Whereas the time has come for the dominion government to consider the problem of education as a dominion responsibility, or at least a responsibility wherein federal aid in much greater measure should be given, to assist already burdened and harassed municipal governments;-
I might point out that they do not even mention here the provincial governments in the resolution. They go directly from the federal to the municipal. This is the preamble. Then the preamble reads:
Therefore be it resolved that the Manitoba Associated Chambers of Commerce requests the Canadian Chamber of Commerce to make the strongest representations to the dominion government to persuade it to accept a much larger degree of responsibility regarding the cost of education in the provinces and for such purpose to assist the provinces to a much greater degree with federal aid for education.
I think that resolution speaks for itself. Many resolutions have been passed in the last year or so and are being passed today. If you read them carefully I think you will find that their meaning is not always the same. They do not look upon federal aid to education in the same way. They indicate different conceptions of the meaning of those words which have become almost a slogan in the country.
It would appear that everyone is anxious to maintain provincial autonomy in connection with education. As I said earlier in my remarks, I cannot understand how this resolution as it is now worded could be
compatible with the maintenance of provincial autonomy. Everyone knows that when a government or any other body makes a grant it is bound to exercise some control. Apparently the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) was under some illusion last year when he spoke on this matter. I remember him saying that it could be done easily and simply and he pointed out to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), that that had been done by his department. I should like to quote from page 585 of Hansard of February 22, 1951, where the leader of the opposition is reported as follows, after the minister had just spoken:
The minister who has just spoken is one who has reason to know that these exclusive fields do not always present the constitutional barriers where there is an attempt or when there is a definite plan to assist in a particular way.
And again:
But I would point out that just as education is the exclusive field of jurisdiction of the provincial government so is hospitalization, except for marine hospitalization. Nevertheless, no insuperable barrier has been encountered by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), to find a way to assist the hospitals of this country, and hospitalization generally, where it was found that the provincial governments did have some difficulty in that field.
Then he goes on to say:
I would go further. These plans have been carried forward in many instances without any suggestion that directly or indirectly there was interference with the administrative responsibilities of these provincial departments which handle these particular activities.
Apparently his illusion has been dispelled in that regard because yesterday he had definitely changed his views and I quote from his remarks, as reported on page 608 of Hansard:
We have seen what happened in the case of the department of health. Health measures and hospitalization, except for military hospitals, were under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. Little by little the dominion government have entered that field until now they have expanded their department of health to a point where, with publicity agents added, they have an organization that is incomparably larger than that to be found in any of the provinces.
The complaint of the leader of the opposition is that the autonomy of the provinces suffers by the making of grants. Another example in this connection is the aid given to universities. These grants have raised no political controversy, at the time those grants were instituted. Today the leader of the opposition used strong language in referring to the manner in which it was being done and he questioned the wisdom of the government in doing it.
The reason I bring this out at the present time is to show that if the federal government or any government is expected to give
[Mr. Jutras.l

substantial grants to any other body it is bound, irrespective of what the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has just said, to exercise some control over the expenditure of such grants. I am surprised that any hon. member would argue that parliament can make substantial earmarked grants to a province without supervising the manner in which they are expended.
The resolution asks, first, that means be provided to expand education. I do not think any strong argument has been advanced for the federal government invading the educational field which is fundamentally, basically and constitutionally a provincial right. No substantial reason has been offered to warrant the federal government providing means to expand education. I am dealing with the resolution one part at a time. To expand education would mean that you are going to take education with all its irregularities and increase its scope. That is the meaning to be taken from the resolution.
Why could not the provinces do that better than the federal government? All the federal government will be doing will be to go out into the provinces, raise some money and then turn it over to the provinces so that they can raise the standard of education. But that also implies control. If we are to vote money to expand education in the country we have the responsibility of seeing that the money will accomplish that expansion of education.
To merely make a grant to a province, and we make many as it is, does not mean it will be applied to education. I suppose it will be said that the money could be earmarked for education. Even though that is done what is there to prevent a province, not necessarily cutting its own grant to education but being tempted, and perhaps justified, to refrain from increasing that grant. In effect the federal grant would simply replace the provincial grant.
If we vote money to expand education in the country we must of necessity exercise a certain degree of control, at least to the extent of seeing that the money so voted is applied to the expansion of education. The moment you attempt that, you attempt a certain degree of control in education. And that applies only to the expansion. But we see that this resolution deals with another far more complicated, far more involved and far more delicate problem, that of the equalization of education.
I agree with the hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot) that, on that basis particularly, the resolution is premature at this time. I ask you this: how can you expect the federal government to equalize education 55704-42J
Education
when the provinces have not equalized it in their own field? Surely the basis of the first step in the process would be for a province at least to establish a system of equalization within that province before the federal government should be expected to step in to equalize education.
I presume that when the hon. member for Saskatoon refers to equalization he means equalization as between one province and another. Because if he means equalization of education within a province, then definitely it would involve control.

May I suggest to the hon. member that I have never in the house suggested equalization of education anywhere. I have emphasized equalization of opportunity for education. My hon. friend keeps using the term loosely, and in that connection he quotes me incorrectly.
I welcome the interruption but, to tell the truth, it is a pretty fine distinction.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Read the resolution.
Read the resolution.

I have read it twice, and I intend to read it again. But the hon. member will agree that the distinction is a pretty fine one. The resolution contains this expression: "should take into consideration means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity."
That is right.

Well, if the facilities are not there, they will not have much opportunity. I am looking at the problem from the practical point of view-to get something done, not just to talk in generalities. Because if we were to pass this resolution, then surely it is intended to equalize education throughout the country. Otherwise, if it is only a matter of opportunity, and no means is provided, there is not much point in carrying on the discussion. One must face the problem now. The importance of the argument applies to the opportunity as well. I fail to see how any federal government could possibly devise a formula that, to use the expression of the resolution, would equalize educational opportunity across Canada, without going in in some way. It is very difficult for me to understand how this could be done.
That is why I say that, in this equalization, the first step is up to the province. An equalization system should be established first in the province, before any consideration of the federal government should enter into the picture.

Education
Is not the hon. member aware that today every department of education is seeking to equalize opportunity within the province?

That is a broad statement that would require a good deal of qualification. They may have the intent to equalize education, but 'how successful have they been, and to what extent they have made an effort to do it, is still another matter. I am not the only one who holds that view. I believe hon. members of the C.C.F., including the hon. member for Saskatoon and perhaps also the hon. member for York South quoted from this booklet, which purports to be a report on the financing of education in Canada, and to have been prepared at the request of the Alberta teachers association for presentation at the national convention of the Canadian teachers federation at Vancouver on August 13 to 17, 1945. By the way, it was published by the Canadian teachers federation, and I believe a copy of it was sent to me by that organization.
For the information of the hon. member for York South I would say that at page 32, part of section 3 states as follows:
As a means of removing or at least greatly lessening the inequity of Canadian education, three administrative and financial adjustments or reforms are recommended:
1.	For the area of municipal or small district finance-larger units of administration.
2.	For provincial administrative areas-sound equalization schemes supported by adequate provincial funds. These seem urgently needed in all provinces where such schemes are not currently in operation. If, in this field where the provincial governments have undisputed autonomy, thoroughgoing equalization schemes were universal, the reasonableness of proposing an equalization scheme dominion-wide in scope would be greatly increased.
In effect, that is exactly what it means. If a scheme were already established in the provinces, the argument for federal assistance, if one wishes to call it that, would be very much stronger. But, even apart from equalization as such, without going into the matter more fully I would suggest that a great many of the school acts of the provinces have a long way to go before there is equalization of opportunity in education within those provinces.
I could go on for some time on this matter, but I do not propose to do so now. It is obvious, I suggest, that before the federal government could go in to equalize opportunity within a province, a very thorough spring cleaning of some of those school acts would have to be done. One can see the difficulty that would arise at once. So that even if the federal government did want to act at the present time, in certain of the provinces it would be prevented from doing so

because of the obsolete school acts they have on their statute books. I think every hon. member is aware of that fact.
So that I suggest the first thing to do would be to try to direct public opinion along the line of improving education generally in Canada, but that such attention should be centred on the provincial governments instead of on the federal government, and that the people ought not to be distracted from the responsible authority in the matter.
While I realize that the teachers federation are endeavouring to better their condition- and certainly I do not blame them for doing so; indeed I would give them all the support I can, because I believe they have a strong case and should receive better remuneration for the work they do-I suggest sincerely to them that if they would concentrate at the provincial level, at which point they have a chance of bettering their condition, they would have a greater chance of achieving success than by being taken in by this general slogan of federal aid to education. I thought the Manitoba school trustees association made one of the finest presentations to the Rowell-Sirois commission in 1937-38. I would like to put on record their submission on this very point of federal aid to education, which is to be found in volume 9 of the briefs presented to that commission:
The policy, control and' financing of schools, as between dominion and province, is and must remain a provincial responsibility, but certain of the social services and kindred obligations should be considered to be national obligations and the cost thereof assumed and paid by the dominion, thereby leaving the province freer scope to care for the needs of education.
That, I think, was a very sound approach. I believe almost everyone who has taken part in this discussion has approached the question on the basis that education is a provincial responsibility and must remain such. Then why not free the hands of the provinces to apply more of their resources to education? In passing I might suggest that this recommendation has been followed very closely by the federal government since that time. As we all know, this is exactly what the federal government has been trying to do. It has relieved the provinces to a large extent of their responsibilities in connection with social services, with the result that the provinces should be in a better position to meet their educational requirements.
At the same time I want to quote the conclusions of the Sirois report itself. I still think that was one of the soundest reports ever published in Canada and that with very few exceptions their conclusions have proved

to be correct. On this complex and delicate matter of federal aid to education the report had this to say at page 51 of book II:
We have expressed our objection to grants for elementary and secondary education where any suspicion of dominion interference would seem to us dangerous.
So it seems advisable not to institute a system of grants or assistance at the primary or secondary school level, if we are to maintain provincial autonomy in the field of education.
In this resolution the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) advocates expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose. As I said earlier, it is almost impossible to conceive of a formula that would accomplish this expansion and equalization without at the same time involving some measure of control over these things. As a matter of fact for any government, federal or provincial, to make a grant to any body without exercising any control whatever would in itself be an evasion of responsibility.
In presenting their arguments a great many hon. members have based them on the assumption that the provinces did not have the financial resources to carry out this expansion and equalization.

Previously I quoted Mr. Argue, associate professor of education at the university of Alberta. I would like to put on record just four more sentences from what he had to say on this point. It will take only a minute, and will not make very much
Education
difference. I will not go into it beyond saying they made a complete survey of the situation and here is what they said on that score:
It was also indicated, however, that the majority of the provinces could have provided much more adequately for their schools than they did in 1941 without federal aid and without reserving more than a "reasonably attainable" proportion of their public revenues for the schools.

Mr. Speaker, this resolution reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada, by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose.
This is a very interesting resolution. If we analyse the history of "federal aid" to education in Canada during the first half of the twentieth century, it is apparent that "federal aid" as it exists has come about now in a very orderly manner by agreement with the provinces. The first act of "federal aid" was when Sir Robert Borden came to office with a Conservative government during the period from 1911 to 1917. I refer to the Agricultural Instruction Act passed in 1913 under which the sum of $10 million was allotted, to be spent during the following ten years. The next legislative enactment concerning "federal aid" came under the same prime minister in 1919, when the Technical Education Act was placed upon the statute books. This statute also allotted $10 million for technical education and again provided that the money should be paid over a period of ten years thereafter. Therefore during the Borden regime we had the sum of $20 million allotted by statute for federal aid to education, the first $10 million for agricultural training and the second $10 million for technical education. This was no small accomplishment in those days when the population of Canada was about half the size that it is now.
Next, we come to another Conservative regime, namely that of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen. We find then a great absence of any further expansion of "federal aid" to education. The next Conservative regime was that of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. We find then a great effort to provide further "federal aid" to education, but no result. I mention the Vocational Education Act passed in 1931. Hon. members who are longer in public life than I am may recall that that act provided $750,000 per year for the purpose of vocational education, and the period of operation of the act was to be fifteen years. To say the least, under the Meighen and Bennett regimes, advancement of federal aid to education "perished in the attempt" along with somebody else.

Education
We come now to the regime ol the late Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King and that of our present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). In placing those two regimes together for consideration, I can mention to the house the Youth Training Act passed in 1939. This statute was operative for a three-year period following its passage, and provided $4,500,000 in "federal aid" to train rural and urban young people in the latter days of the depression. Then, in 1942 a Liberal government under the late Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King passed the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act of that year. This statute was the means of repealing, in effect, the Youth Training Act of 1939 and the defunct Vocational Education Act of the Bennett regime passed in 1931.
A very significant accomplishment can be placed on record under the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act. From 1945 down to the end of the present fiscal year the Department of Labour reports that it will have spent or will be spending on all the various types of vocational training under the statute in question the sum of $51,541,625. Now, this sum is in addition to the "federal aid" to universities provided in the estimates at the last session, which amounted to $7,100,000. This makes a total for these purposes in the post-war period from 1945 down to the present fiscal year by way of "federal aid" to education of $58,641,625.
Summarizing "federal aid" to education in terms of dollars, Mr. Speaker, we see that during the first half of the twentieth century Sir Robert Borden was responsible for allotting $20 million. The Right Hon. Arthur Meighen is responsible for allotting nothing, and the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett tried to allot much but wound up by spending nothing. You have, therefore, $20 million to the credit of the Conservative party in those days. To me this does not sound like the words of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) who said that the policy of his party was "federal assistance ever".
I think, however, that under Liberal governments we have done much. I am not underestimating the federal aid to education at the university level of $7,100,000, the byproduct of the Massey commission on arts, letters and sciences. I think that is all to the good. In these days when we find difficult problems within and without for all Canadians, a discussion of the humanities cannot be properly conducted under this resolution. I do say that is a significant achievement, and it is one that is very near and dear to me.
What I wish to stress tonight is the continuing need of vocational training, and the

aid which this government in particular has given to vocational training for those who do not go to university either through their own choice or otherwise. Youth training today at the vocational training school level is a matter of vital importance to those who do not choose a profession or the advanced lines of business which require a university or other education. It is for them that I speak tonight, and it is for them that I encourage the government in the increase it has seen fit to make in the vocational training estimates of the Department of Labour.
In the year 1952-53, I find in the estimates of the Department of Labour, under the heading "Youth Training" the sum of $440,000. I am gratified to note an increase in that item over the year 1951-52, because in that year it amounted to $410,000. I pass on to apprenticeship training under the vocational training branch of the Department of Labour. I am gratified to note that in the year 1952-53 there is $750,000 in the estimates for this purpose, whereas in the year 1951-52 there was $500,000. This constitutes an increase of $250,000. As to vocational school assistance, it is a matter of satisfaction to see that in the estimates this year we have $2 million, the same amount as last year. Fore-manship training is a matter which is going to receive attention, and there is an increase there over last year. I note the sum of $12,000 for the coming year. There is also a further item in these estimates as to vocational training for "gainful employment"or defence industries. Here we have the sum of $650,000, an increase of $150,000 over last year. Hon. members will be pleased to note further that the vocational training branch of the Department of Labour proposes to continue its work of training workers for the armed forces. Under this item we have $160,000 in the estimates for the coming year. There is a final item for vocational correspondence courses amounting to $15,000.
It is apparent therefore that in the year 1952-53 in the Department of Labour there is allotted the sum of $4,027,000 for vocational training. Last year, 1951-52, there was $3,652,000. This is a formidable increase of some $375,000.
Why do I take such satisfaction in the increase of these sums? It is because in the riding of Toronto Rosedale I speak for many middle-class families and also for those in the lower brackets. They feel the need for opportunity in education along the lines of vocational training. It is a particular satisfaction for me to know that vocational training facilities in Canada, under the proven methods established in the first half of this

century, are going to be expanded and that there will be an expansion of educational opportunities in the vocational training field for the children of these particular families.
I note that the department is skilled in the administration of this "federal aid" for vocational training. I feel that there will be a judicious handling of the money so that organized labour may not fear an extraordinary production of the wrong kind of workers in the wrong places. Experience has shown in the past that this branch has done its work well in co-operation with the provinces. As evidence of my interest in this vocational training problem, hon. members may have noted that there is on the order paper resolution No. 13 which reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give early consideration to the making of provision for increased financial assistance for the improvement and extension of vocational training facilities and the training of workers in skilled trades and occupations, with a view to providing adequate facilities and opportunities for training for workers in all sections of Canada and developing and increasing the skills and numbers of workers in essential trades and occupations in the national interest.
We come now, Mr. Speaker, to the present resolution. In attempting to explain the gradual development of "federal aid" to education, one asks one's self the question: How does it come about that under the Borden regime we had some federal aid? How do we explain the great absence of "federal aid" and no expansion of the accepted lines of federal aid under the Meighen and the Bennett regimes? The best explanation that I can offer is the opinion of a noteworthy, now deceased journalist in this country-and I refer to Mr. J. W. Dafoe-in a letter which he wrote on September 16, 1943, a copy of which appears in the "Historical Review" of 1944. In this letter the late Mr. Dafoe, who is respected by most Canadians, said of Sir Robert Borden:
His stature rises as the perspective lengthens but it has some way to go yet before justice is done him. I had many a heart-to-heart talk with him down the years, and after each of them I was in the habit of saying to myself: "Either he's a Grit in disguise or I'm a Tory."
Passing on, we can sum up the situation to date in this way. At the university level the Liberal government of the day has allotted $7,100,000; at the vocational training school level since 1945 there is the sum of $51,541,000. The question is what is to be done by way of "federal aid" for education at the grade school and secondary school level.
I was deeply impressed this afternoon with the statesmanlike speech of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson). To my way of thinking he gave hon. members much to consider
Education
at this time, when attempts are made on all sides, shall I say, to strain the constitution, in spirit and letter, to the very limit. He made a deep impression upon me in many ways, but more particularly with reference to the province of Ontario in which I reside.
X am not as familiar as is the Minister of Justice with what went on in the province of Ontario during the regime of the premier who preceded the present incumbent of that office. I note with interest, however, that the minister is able to establish that, during that regime, more attention was paid to bridges and roads than to education, as the figures of the province show. During his speech it came to my mind that today we had certain aspects of the dominion-provincial-tax situation still with us in the province of Ontario. On March 1, 1952, in the well known magazine Saturday Night an exemplary journalist by the name of Michael Barkway wrote an interesting article on what he calls "Tax Impasse Costing Millions". There is a subheading which reads: "Ontario, Quebec aloof from first Ottawa tax offer, consider new one". This is a detailed study of the situation of Ontario finances in so far as this relationship is concerned with the federal government. Hon. members will no doubt feel that they do not want me to go into detail at this time, and I do not wish to do so. But Mr. Barkway reaches this conclusion, and I quote him in the middle of the article:
. . . and it is already certain that over the whole five-year period Ontario will have lost substantial revenue by staying out of the federal-provincial agreements.
If this is so, Mr. Speaker, may I conclude with this thought. The present incumbent of the premiership of the province of Ontario has proven himself to be a co-operative man, and a conciliatory man in every sense of the word. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) seems concerned about the opportunity for educational advancement in this country, and I include the province of Ontario within the meaning of his words in this house. Let him and the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) use their influence with the premier of Ontario to cause him to sign a tax agreement and stop the loss of money described by the journalist which I have just quoted. Within the framework of the dominion-provincial tax arrangements, if we can cause the provinces to make the necessary agreements, let us give whatever tax funds the provinces may need for all purposes, including that of education. But, Mr. Speaker, the constitution of Canada in the field of education is to me sacrosanct, as I know it to be with the majority of Canadians. I speak not only of its letter but of its spirit. The

Education
best evidence of the fact that we must therefore carefully seek out agreements before we attempt to adopt legislation such as this in its entirety lies in the variety of views which have been expressed here in this debate. As the last speaker has said, let us preserve provincial autonomy. I say: Let us have federal aid to education, as now existing for universities and vocational training establishments, but at the grade school level and the secondary school level it is for the provinces to administer within the framework of the provinces under dominion-provincial agreements as visualized by the Minister of Justice this afternoon.
However I am satisfied and proud of the federal aid given at the university and vocational training levels. On this question I will not add anything else. But I will ask hon. members not to lose sight of the constitution when they advocate "federal aid" to education at the grade and secondary school levels.

Mr. Speaker, we have before us the following resolution moved by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight):
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada, by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose.
The first thing that comes to mind, on reading this resolution, is the matter of whether education is a federal or a provincial responsibility. According to our constitution, education is under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. One must therefore conclude that the above resolution, as was so aptly put by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), is premature. Furthermore, we are not here to find ways of avoiding and circumventing the law, but actually to pass wise laws and to see to their enforcement by making sure we ourselves are setting a good example.
As to autonomy, I am pleased to state in this house what I have said several times, at Jonquiere and at Arvida. Furthermore, on December 14, 1949, as a member of a delegation in my capacity as mayor, I requested from the prime minister of the province of Quebec, municipal autonomy for my city stating that any municipal authority should have the right to impose taxes to be able to meet its own obligations and remain free. I pointed out also that the functions of administrators did not consist solely in begging from IMr. Henry.]
the superior authorities a few dollars owed to them, but in devoting all their energies, their zeal and devotion to the accomplishment of administrative actions worthy of the name, in the common interest.
For such reasons, if taxing powers in the field of education are to be defined as between the federal and provincial governments, and likewise if agreements are to be made to amend the constitution in this regard, let that be done without delay. But as long as this is not done, I shall oppose this resolution with all my might and I want to say so frankly and honestly in this house.
